TREATMENT OP MILITARY AND CIVILIAN PRISONERS BY JAPANESE On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Kingdom secretary of state for foreign affairs made the following statement in the House of Commons at Westminster to-day in reply to an inquiry regarding the treatment of military prisoners and civilians by the Japanese army at Hong Kong after its capitulation:
Out of regard for the feelings of the thousands of relations of the victims, his majesty's government have been unwilling to publish any accounts of Japanese atrocities at Hong Kong until these had been confirmed beyond any possibility of doubt.
His Majesty's government are now in possession of statements by reliable eye witnesses who succeeded in escaping from Hong Kong towards the end of January or early in February. Their testimony established the fact that Japanese army at Hong Kong perpetrated against their helpless military prisoners and civil population, without distinction of race or colour, the same kind of barbarities which aroused the horror of the civilized world at the time of the Nanking massacre of 1937.
It is known that fifty officers and men of the British were bound hand and foot and then bayoneted to death. It is known that ten days after capitulation wounded were still being collected from the hills and Japanese were refusing permission to bury the dead. It is known that women, both Asiatic and European, were raped and murdered and that one entire Chinese district was declared a brothel, regardless of status of inhabitants.
All the survivors of the garrison including Indian, Chinese and Portuguese have been herded into a camp consisting of wrecked huts without doors, windows, light or sanitation. By the end of January 150 cases of dysentery had occurred but no drugs or medical facilities were supplied. The dead had to be buried in a corner of the camp. The Japanese guards are utterly callous and the repeated requests of General Maltby, the general officer commanding, for an interview with the Japanese commander have been curtly refused. This presumably means that the Japanese high command have connived at the conduct of their forces. The Japanese government stated at the end of February that numbers of prisoners in Hong Kong were British 5,072, Canadian 1,689, Indian 3,829, others 357, total 10,947.
Most of the European residents, including some who are seriously ill, have been interned, and like the military prisoners are being given only a little rice and water and occasionally scraps of other food.
There is some reason to believe that conditions have been slightly improved since date on which the eye-witnesses, whom I have quoted, escaped, but Japanese government have refused their consent to visit to Hong Kong of a repre-
sentative of protecting power and no permission has yet been granted for such a visit by representative of International Red Cross Committee. They have in fact announced that they require all foreign consuls to withdraw from all territories they have invaded since the outbreak of the war. It is clear that their treatment of prisoners and civilians will not bear independent investigation.
I have no information as to condition of our prisoners of war and civilians in Malaya. The only report available is a statement by Japanese official news agency of March 3 stating that 77,699 Chinese have been arrested and subjected to what is described as "a severe examination." It is not difficult to imagine what that entails.
I am sorry that I have had to make such a statement to the house. Two things will be clear from it, to the house, to the country and to the world. The J apanese claim that their forces are animated by a lofty code of chivalry, l>ushido, is a nauseating hypocrisy. That is the first. The second is that the enemy must be utterly defeated. The house will agree with me that we can best express our sympathy with the victims of these appalling outrages by redoubling our efforts to ensure his utter and overwhelming defeat.
That is the end of Mr. Eden's statement. I am informed by our high commissioner in London that on the basis of information so far received, United Kingdom authorities agree that of all the reports of specific atrocities received1 to date none are alleged to have been committed against Canadians, but no reports show that in so far as general treatment of prisoners of war is concerned Japanese have made any differentiation between Canadians and other British troops.
Words cannot begin to express the sense of outrage and the feeling of bitter resentment to which this announcement of Japanese atrocities at Hong Kong is certain to give rise among civilized! peoples everywhere, and nowhere more than in the different countries of the British empire and in the United States with which Japan is at war.
Retribution for barbaric behaviour of the kind will follow in full measure in due course. Meanwhile, numbers of Canadians, both soldiers and civilians, in Hong Kong and in other parts of the far east, are now and will continue for some time to be at the mercy of the Japanese forces. Remembering this fact, it is of the utmost importance that no act of vengeance should be permitted or taken against persons of Japanese origin in our country, since any such acts might be made an excuse for acts of retaliation upon Canadian soldiers or citizens in the orient.
I may add that the Canadian government, in conjunction with the governments of Australia, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, have been and are making every effort, both through the countries which are protecting their interests in enemy coun-

tries and through the International Red Cross, to get into personal touch with prisoners of war and others. The object of all these inquiries is twofold: to secure all possible authentic information, and also to bring such measure of relief in the nature of medical supplies, food and personal comforts as can possibly be arranged.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the facts related by Mr. Eden and detailed to this House of Commons will shock the whole world. But they will help us to renew our determination to end forever those systems of government under which such atrocities and barbarities are permitted to occur. I should like to express this further thought. Reprisals are unthinkable to those of us who believe in the Christian way of life; and I would sound a note of warning-that reprisals against Japanese nationals in Canada must not be contemplated. Let it never be forgotten that there are still Canadians and British in the hands of the Japanese foe.

I should like to add a word to what has already been said. I am sure the recital we have just heard has filled each one of us with horror. The day must come when the officers and governments who have been responsible for these atrocities must be brought to the bar of justice and dealt with in a fitting manner.
I too would join with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) in expressing the hope that however much our people may be provoked against the Japanese, nowhere in Canada may there be any untoward act which would, as has already been said, give an excuse to the devilish men who are wreaking this kind of treatment upon those who are simply carrying on their activities both military and civil in war time in a fitting way. I cannot help thinking that the civilized world, which is shocked now,' ought to have been equally shocked when similar outrages were committed at Nanking. That, however, is in the past, and I join in the expressions of horror and resentment expressed by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition.

In times like these it is easy for us to be unwise. The all-important thing for us to keep in mind is this, that because of mishaps, misconceptions and mismanagement in the past the British empire has allowed itself to become so weak that these things have been made possible. We are suffering from the results of our past mistakes. We cannot in any way
atone for them, or extricate ourselves from the difficulties into which they have plunged us, by making others. The thing for us to do is to keep our minds calm and to concentrate with all the power of our being on the things we can do to retrieve ourselves from the disaster into which we are plunged. Certainly one of the things we should not do is indulge in any untoward act toward any national of Japanese origin in this country.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word in the circumstances? I should like to ask the leaders of the first three parties who have spoken whether there has been the least suggestion from anyone in British Columbia, or in Canada, that we should take any action against Japanese which would invite retaliation or which could in even the faintest degree be comparable to the brutalities about which we have heard. What we have tried to do is to get the government to take steps, before it is too late, to protect our wives and children in British Columbia from atrocities that may come upon us.

Mr. Speaker, I agree that the problem before us is a serious one, and I agree with what has been said by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other groups. But I do wish to point out that members from British Columbia almost unanimously have tried to impress upon the government this very fact about which they have spoken. My information last night at 11 o'clock was that only some 700 Japanese have been moved from British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has pointed out, some of us have our wives and children or families out there. We want to impress upon the government what the situation is. So far the government has not taken it seriously enough. It is not that we are advocating reprisals. But the government must bear the responsibility, and it is a most serious responsibility, if they do it well. We do not advocate reprisals; we deprecate them, and will do everything in our power to prevent any. But the government must wake up to the seriousness of the situation.
Order.

I might say a lot
more than I have, but I want to ask a question, which I am entitled to do, on the orders of the day-and I am more serious than I have ever been before with respect to anything I have said in this house. How many Japanese have been moved from the province of British Columbia since December 7?

SINKING OF VESSELS OFF NOVA SCOTIA COAST On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. As a member for a Nova Scotia coast constituency I want to ask whether reports are correct that several cargo ships have recently been sunk within sight of the Nova Scotia coast, and what steps are being taken to protect this coast and ships plying along it.
Hon. ANGUS A. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): I have just received notice of my hon. friend's question. In reply to the first part of it I can say it is true that ships have been sunk not far distant from the Nova Scotia coast. As to the second part, namely, what steps are being taken to protect this coast and the ships plying along it, I do not think that that is the sort of question to which a detailed public answer could be made. All I can say to my hon. friend is that steps are being taken, and that every facility at the command of the naval service and the Royal Canadian Air Force to guard our coastal waters is being used.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson), which I take to be of some importance in its general application. I have here the serial number of a tractor which was sold to a farmer in August, 1940. Under protest the purchaser paid a tax on this tractor of $70.80. I have as well a letter from an officer of the Department of National Revenue which states that this tractor was cleared through customs in April, 1940, and as such would not be subject to the war exchange tax. I have also the serial number of a second tractor that was purchased in 1940 and on which a tax of S66.20 was paid. I am not certain of the date on which this second tractor was cleared IMr. Cniiokshank.l
through customs, but I think it was early in the spring of 1940. I have also on my desk an article printed in a local newspaper which in effect states that some companies, or at least a company, imported large quantities of farm implements before the imposition of the war exchange tax. These implements have been kept in stock and apparently the policy has been practised of adding the amount of the war exchange tax to the price of the implements.
I would put my question to the minister in this way. First, has the department any knowledge which would lead it to believe that the practice just referred to has been followed by any farm implement company or companies? Second, will the department take steps to determine the correctness or otherwise of the assertion made? Third, if this tax was added to the price of the machinery, was the money so collected paid to the treasury? Fourth, if the tax was collected and not paid to the treasury, will the department take steps to (a) secure the money so collected for the benefit of the treasury, or (b) require the implement company or companies to reimburse the purchaser the amount of the tax so collected?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton West) for the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) made his statement on this bill I moved the adjournment of the debate. I wish now to make a few references to this measure. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has stated that by arrangement these three measures are to be more or less considered at the same time, so that any reference I may make to Bill No. 12 or to Bill No. 14 will be quite in order.
At the outset I should like to register a protest, as I have on former occasions, against the bringing down so late in the season of measures affecting the agricultural interests in western Canada. The farmers will have to change their programmes more or less to meet the provisions of the measures that will pass this house. This is March 10. Seeding will be taking place in another two or three weeks. Last year it was May before we finally decided on the regulations with respect to the wheat acreage reduction. It is hardly fair to ask the farmer to change his whole programme a few days before he starts seeding.
I believe that Bill No. 14 and Bill No. 12 could be proceeded with with considerable haste. Bill No. 13, the one I am speaking to particularly now, deals with the matter of price. As the farmer will not be affected by the provisions of this bill until next fall, I think we should take considerable time to consider it in committee. I do not think it is necessary that this bill should be reported back from committee as soon as the others. In committee we should have a good deal more information than we have had about this whole problem of wheat marketing, prices, and so on.
I think we are all agreed wheat is the chief commodity produced in Saskatchewan. In that province we have what might be termed a wheat economy. If you will consider the part that wheat plays in our national income you will realize the importance that should be attached to it. Only about five per cent of the national income goes to twenty per cent of the population of Canada who are depending on agriculture in western Canada. I think you will realize that there is something wrong. I hardly think I need state my position again. On many occasions I have gone on record in this house, and I think it is well understood just where I stand. I think I can say that my position is such that I have been the greatest champion of the producers of western Canada in this house. For fourteen consecutive sessions I have been a greater champion than any other member from western Canada.
It was very interesting for me to listen yesterday to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) make the somersault that he did. I recall that last year he supported 70-cent wheat, but yesterday he would not stop at 90 cents. No, sir; he would not establish the economy of western Canada on a basis of 90-cent wheat but would go up to $1.25 a bushel. I hope that when this bill comes back from the committee he will still be of the same mind and give that price his support.

Wheat Board Act

However, he wound up by saying that he would support these measures which the government brought down yesterday.

speechtext: He is just outbidding the others.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Of course he is, and I hope he backs it up when the time comes.
Agriculture in this country entered the war in 1939 at practically an all-time low. It had taken a count of nine and was in no condition to stand the count of ten and a knockout. But if we compare the state of agriculture in Canada with agriculture in the United States in 1939 when we entered the war, it will be realized that agriculture in the United States entered the war in a much better condition than we did in Canada, and has been dealt with more generously since. The United States are still continuing to look after agricultural producers in that country. I have a report here from Chicago, dated March 3 of this year, which states that the Commodity Credit Corporation of the United States has insisted- that there shall be no further sales from the "ever normal" granary. They are not worrying about their surplus.
Great Britain, too, has been looking after its farmers. I have a report here from Liverpool stating that there will be an increased price of 161 cents a bushel to the British farmer to encourage production in that country.
I recall, as will other hon. members, that in 1935 during the discussion on the Canadian Wheat Board Act which we are amending to-day, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett made the statement and produced figures to show that western Canada had produced in the preceding six years six billion dollars of new wealth, and he added that a country or any part of a country which was capable of that great production was a country worth saving. I hurl those. remarks across the floor of this house to-day and say that the possibilities that exist in western Canada of producing a vast 'amount of new wealth annually makes it a country well worth while saving.
In western Canada we must stick to our wheat economy; for if we in the prairie provinces undertook instead to produce live stock to our full capacity, agriculture in Ontario and possibly throughout Canada would be ruined. So I say that we must not replace our wheat economy in the west by any other production policy.
I have one or two suggestions to make. In view of the present critical stage of this war and of what is taking place throughout the world, I submit that speculation on the stock and grain exchanges should cease immediately. Indeed it should have ceased when the war started. Costs of production,

transportation, marketing, and every other feature of our price structure affecting the agricultural life of Canada, should be maintained as near to normal costs as possible, so that the greatest efforts on the part of our producers can be exerted at the least possible expenditure. As to retail prices, instead of talking so much about a ceiling, the government should put retail prices, or a great number of them, back to where they belong until parity is brought about with the prices of farm products.
The Minister of Agriculture yesterday made a clear-cut statement and gave a detailed review of the situation of agriculture. He went on to speak of the prices of cattle, hogs, butter, eggs, cheese, and so on, for all of which I commend him, although the credit is not due to him alone. There is a war on; there is a demand for these farm products; our western farmers promptly responded to that demand, and a great deal of the credit is due to them. Certainly with a war on prices must advance and have advanced.
The minister also reviewed farm income in Canada. He said-I hope he is right in his mathematics-that there will be a considerable increase in 1942 in individual farm incomes. In connection with his Bill No. 12, he stated that he was endeavouring to hold the acreage seeded to wheat this year around the twenty million mark. I think that is quite a reasonable figure, because with the increase in summer-fallow last year and the decreased acreage seeded to wheat, it is only reasonable to expect that we shall not exceed twenty million acres in wheat this year. If we have an average crop from that acreage it is quite possible that there will be no difficulty in absorbing all the wheat that will come on the market.
The minister also referred to vegetable oils. He emphasized the importance of encouraging the producers of stock, cattle, hogs and so on, in order that animal fats might be available. I shall leave any further reference to that part of his remarks to the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who sits immediately in front of me, except to say that the hon. member for Danforth was about four years ahead of his time in the suggestions he made to the government about vegetable oils, and I claim that I was about three years ahead of my time in many of the suggestions I advanced with respect to the price of wheat and what our wheat policy should be.
May I refer briefly to the farmers' delegation which visited Ottawa in the early part of February last? They made a very reasonable presentation of their case, and their recommendations were undoubtedly fair. I have here a copy of their brief, but I shall refer to only a few paragraphs.

First they referred to farm income. They showed that during the period from 1926 to 1929 farm income in the three prairie provinces amounted to $530,000,000. Since that date and up to last year there was a very considerable reduction in farm income, and they estimated that with a reasonable return in 1942 there might be only $338,000,000 of farm income in the west. They also pointed out that owing to the importance of wheat to Saskatchewan that province had probably suffered most from the decrease in farm income, and to emphasize the importance of wheat to Saskatchewan they showed that while for the year ended July 31, 1941, there was a cash income from all farm products in the province of $180,000,000, seventy-one per cent of that amount, or $129,000,000, came from wheat. That emphasized the importance of wheat in relation to farm income in Saskatchewan.
They also pointed out in. their brief, very fairly, I think, that this government dealt with war industry on a cost-plus basis and a fair return on the capital invested, and they considered that the farmer should be treated in somewhat the same manner. I think that is only a fair request.
Then they point out, what I believe also Is reasonable, that too much emphasis is being placed on the fact that we have these carryovers every year running between four and five hundred million bushels. Because too much emphasis is placed on that, I believe the pool was right in calling it to the attention of the government. Then the pool suggest a one dollar initial price, with a participation which would bring it to a parity, whatever that might be. I think they were reasonable in asking for that. They concluded by stating that if their recommendations were accepted by the government, as regards the segregating of the 1942 crop and the setting of a reasonable price, it would be unnecessary further to restrict the wheat acreage in the west, but that the farmer would govern himself accordingly and would have an opportunity of running his own affairs, so to speak.
Other organizations from western Canada have been making representations to the government, I have here the brief presented by the grain trade-the North-West Line elevators association. These gentlemen go a little further than the pool, because they ask for $1.02 net for the farmer. It was interesting to me to read that, because I recall how strongly, when they were down here in 1935, they opposed the Canada wheat board act as we were framing it then, and threw difficulties in the way of Mr. McFarland for two or three years while he was attempting to support the market; they had no regard for any policies 44561-75J
of that kind. Yet now they are asking for $1.02 net to the farmer. It will be interesting to see whether the government will listen to them. I believe they have some friends in the cabinet.
Another very important document which I have here is the resolution introduced by the Saskatchewan government and passed by the legislature which is now in session, endorsing the representation which was made by the delegation of 430 who attended here in February. That, too, is interesting. It may be significant that the premier of Saskatchewan thought it necessary to fly to Ottawa and muster the Liberal members from that province. He did not see fit to call in any other western members of parliament, but he got together the Liberal members; apparently they had been kicking over the traces. He came down here and assisted the Minister of Agriculture; they went into caucus half a dozen times-I know there was a lot of movement around here-and they backed up their minister; at least they put a little intestinal fortitude into him. It would have been interesting had the minister recited to this house some of the discussions which took place with the wheat committee of the cabinet and the price control board. I understand that the minister threatened that if he did not get his way- and I am glad he is taking this attitude now- he might come across here and present the case from this side of the house. I do not know whether we would have agreed to take him in; however, knowing some of those from western Canada who were associated with him, and watching what has gone on in this house, I do not think we would have wished him to bring over to this side any of the other hon. gentlemen opposite.
I have here however a statement of the hon. gentleman in 1939, when, on May 5, speaking in this chamber in support of Bill No. 83, he quoted Professor Hope of Saskatchewan university to show that the farmer should get 95 cents net on the farm in order to meet the farm debt in western Canada and to carry on in a normal way. I see that now, two or three years later, he is coming around to that idea, but he does not go as far as he did when he suggested that it should be 95 cents net to the farmer.
I also have here statements made by the minister in October. There is a long report in the Regina Leader-Post of October 9 and October 14, wherein, speaking in western Canada, he assured the farmers that they were going to get a lot more for their wheat under the 1942 policy. But I am not going to read these statements, because he would challenge their accuracy; he would say that the press
Wheat Board Act

had misunderstood him and put a wrong interpretation on the language he used

 because that is what he usually does. But the statement is there.
When the delegation of 430 farmers came here in February they thought, from what the Minister of Agriculture said from time to time, they were going to get dollar wheat. They asked for a parity price; and that is what we want. I have here the Searle index, showing that, taking the year 1913-14 as the index year, 147 items stand at 151 and wheat stands at 58. Surely we will admit that there is something wrong there.. We want the parity price; that is what the pool asked for.
If you will add all the bonuses which the farmers of western Canada received during the crop year 1941 to the price received for the 1941 crop-I have here the figures tabled by the minister in answer to certain questions which I put on the order paper-you will find that the government have paid out some $36,000,000 on three particular bonuses. A considerable amount is yet to be paid, however, on that income bonus which was to be disbursed in December. It was to be a Christmas present, but all of it is not yet paid. But, giving the minister credit for all that, there is no way that he can use mathematics to make the farmer of western Canada-who knows-believe that he has received a dollar a bushel for the 1941 crop. They are not all fools out there, by any means, and you have to use some different system of arithmetic to convince them that they have received that much. Especially' is that so-and this is an important thing which has not been taken into consideration in the discussion-if you allow for the estimated loss which the farmer has to sustain on the lower seeded acreage. Six or seven million acres less was seeded to wheat last year. If you estimate that at ten bushels to the acre at fifty cents a bushel, there is a loss of $30 million. There is no allowance either for the extra summer-fallowing of this land; and as the minister, who is a farmer, knows, it costs considerable to summer-fallow.
The farmers will do their part, as they have done in the past, but they should be given a fair price and left to carry on their business according to their own arrangements and their individual methods of farming. Last year many farmers were paid to do things which they would have done in any event. I may just cite my own case. I had' planned to summer-fallow so much, a lot more than I needed to do under the bonus system, but that is what I intended to do. And I know many other farmers who had1 planned to put their farming on a fifty-fifty basis and were paid for doing so under this system. I do not think they wanted that.

I should like to ask the minister what further orders in council, if any, there are going to be to carry out this policy. The minister said yesterday that in connection with Bill No. 13 there would have to be a considerable number of orders in council. We should know what they are. The bill only makes two verbal changes-one is from "seventy" to "ninety", and the other adds the word "mills".

It is not my intention to delay the house very long in connection with this question of wheat, because we will have ample opportunity to deal with the matter when these bills go to committee. Every hon. member from Saskatchewan is interested in the wheat question. We are interested in it for several reasons. First of all, Saskatchewan grows more wheat than any other province in Canada. The second reason is that the whole economy of Saskatchewan is built around wheat. We may, in fact we do, grow other things; we indulge in other forms of agriculture, but our chief agricultural product is wheat.
Let me illustrate what I mean by placing on record a few figures. In 1940 all farm produce of Saskatchewan was valued at $173,000,000, while the value of wheat alone was $132,000,000; in other words about 76 per cent of our agricultural activity was devoted to the production of wheat. In 1941 our total production of agricultural products was valued at $180,000,000, while that of wheat products alone stood at $128,000,000, or 71 per cent.
I would emphasize, too, that there are certain portions of Saskatchewan which can grow nothing but wheat, and there are other areas, such as park lands, where other farm products are grown. But on the great open plains, where most of the wheat is grown, there is no other activity, and there is no other crop we can grow except wheat. When we cannot grow wheat, we cannot grow anything at all. Recause of that, those of us who are members of the house, and happen to live in that area are interested in wheat and in every angle of the question as it presents itself to us.
Since 1929 the wheat problem has worried the House of Commons. Every year we have looked forward to legislation of one kind or another. It has become a hardy annual. Every government has brought down legislation of some kind, but it has been only temporary, effective from year to year. That has been the procedure since 1929.
When the war began in 1939 we in western Canada, as wheat growers, thought that all our difficulties were solved. We thought, "We are through with them now. All the wheat growers' problems will be solved." But we soon found out that this war was not like the last one; it was absolutely different. There was no demand for our wheat. Instead of our wheat problem growing less and less, it has grown greater and greater. The export of wheat to the markets of the world grew smaller and smaller, and each year since the
Wheat Board Act

war began we have seen our wheat piling up more and more, until at the present time we have a large surplus,
Canada has in sight now something like
480,000,000 bushels. We expect to have a carryover of about 400,000,000 bushels. But that is not all there is in the world to-day. We expect the carryover in the Argentine will be about 234 or 235 million bushels, in Australia about 162 million bushels, and in * the United States 610 to 6S0 million bushels. These make in all about a billion and a half bushels of wheat which we expect to have at the end of this crop year.
In our best exporting years we never exported more than 800 or 900 million bushels, and in many years of late we have not exported more than 500 million bushels. In fact in the last few years it has been less than 500 million bushels. It will be seen at once that we have in sight now what may appear to be all the wheat we shall be able to export in the next three years-two years, anyway. That is the problem which we must face; it is the one which confronts the wheat growers at the present time.
Naturally we ask ourselves what would happen if the government were not supporting the price of wheat. If all this wheat were to be thrown on the world's markets, where would the price go? Why, it would likely be worse than it was in 1932, when John I. McFarland was handling the wheat problem for R. B. Bennett. That was the time when it went down to 38 cents Fort William, or 19 cents at the farm.

They were not listening to him then. I ask the house this question: What would happen to our wheat if the government were to withdraw its support? In guaranteeing, as it has, the initial payment to the farmer of western Canada, the government has been doing useful and helpful work. It has cost a large amount of money. The minister told us the other day that the maintenance of the prices for the crops of 1938, 1939 and 1940 had cost $79,900,000. I suppose by this time, with the added interest, it will have reached $80,000,000. That was the cost for those three years.
In dealing with the wheat problem there are three questions we should ask ourselves, ques-

tions which are of grave importance. First of all it is essential that the man who has wheat should receive a price which will assure him a respectable living. The man who has a crop of wheat should have a price from the government or from someone which will assure him a reasonably decent living. There is no doubt about that.
The second point is this. The man who cultivates land and then through an act of Providence receives no return from it should be protected. Providence may step in, and it may develop that either through climatic conditions such as drought or hail, or through a plague of insects such as grasshoppers, saw-flies or cut-worm, through no fault of his own the farmer may lose his crop. Those farmers should be looked after by the government, and in some way a living should be provided for them. It is not the farmer's fault that he has no crop. In my opinion he is more deserving of the sympathy of the government and the people generally than the man who has a crop who at least has something to show for his labour.
The third point to consider is this: What is the government going to do with the wheat when it is delivered? Where are they going to sell it? Where are they going to store it? How much will they pay for storage? These are matters which must be borne in mind when we are dealing with wheat.
Having in mind the three points I have enumerated, I should like to refer to what the government is doing for wheat growers in the present year and' what it proposes to do in the year to come. First of all let us consider the year 1941-42. What has the government's legislation been? First the government has guaranteed an initial payment of 70 cents a bushel, with an additional participating certificate. This is the same provision as was made last year. I am not satisfied with that price; I was not satisfied with it last year. I said at that time that because the cost of living had increased between 10 and 15 per cent the price should be raised to the same extent, up to 78 cents, 80 cents, or somewhere in that neighbourhood. I said that we are entitled1 to that increase in price. I say it again. Labour is getting the increase; why should not the wheat grower receive the same consideration? If 70 cents was a right and proper price two years ago, then 70 cents is not a right and proper price to-day. That is one of the reasons for discontent in western Canada. The price is not quite high enough.
But there are other reasons for discontent, and they are far more important. One hardly ever hears it mentioned, but let me tell the house that in western Canada we have had

Wheat Board Act
one of the worst crop failures in years. So far this year we have marketed only 165,000,000 bushels of wheat, and we expect our total marketings will not go beyondl 200,000,000 bushels. Last year we marketed 455 million bushels. There is quite a difference. The reason for the discontent is the crop failure we had this year in western Canada.
There is another reason-the low grades. These are the things we should look into. In my district, for example, practically all the wheat is combined. A farmer will go out and start his combine to-day and haul his wheat into the elevator and get No. 1 northern for it. During the night rain falls and washes the wheat and when he next goes out he finds this Thatcher wheat has bleached. This is a rust-resistant high grade wheat, but it is apt to bleach. He finds that he can get only No. 2 northern, for that. If there is another rainfall, when he goes out again he finds he will get only No. 3 northern or No. 4. I have received only No. 4 for wheat grown in the same field from which I took wheat that graded No. 1. Nothing had happened to the wheat except washing by rain. I have asked some technical men about this bleached wheat and they assure me that as far as milling or baking qualities are concerned, it is just as good as any other wheat. This man is a member of the grades standard board and he tells me that whenever it meets he has asked that this matter be considered, that this wheat should not be given such low grades. Because of the low grades of wheat this year the average price received by the farmers has been 49 cents Fort William, whereas a year ago it was 52 to 54 cents. The lower grades of wheat caused the lower average price.
That is one thing the government has done. In addition, the government has asked the farmers to market on a quota basis. This is one of the most helpful pieces of legislation we have, ana there has been very little criticism of it from the farmer. They say it is too bad that they did not have it during the good years. They contend that it has taught them how to finance. Previously they hauled their wheat in the fall of the year, received their money, spent it, and then when the spring came around and it was necessary to seed they had to borrow money. They say they do not want to see this quota system done away with; they hope it will be continued.
The next thing the government did was to institute a system of bonuses. The first of these is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which has been in operation for three years. This is one of the most popular pieces of legislation for the farmers of western Canada that this or any other government has placed on the 44561-76
statute book. Outside of the Liberal members, however, it has received scanty support. It has received nothing but adverse criticism from the majority of members of this house, apart from members of the Liberal party. The fact of the matter is that many members went home to the west when this legislation was put through and said that the government would never pay, that it was done only to fool the public, to get their votes. Then when the payment was made, they contended it was done just to fool the people, that no more payments would be made. When the last payment was made they contended that the farmers would never have got it if they had not come down here and raised such a storm and so forced the government to pay. I heard statements like that. I have received hundreds of letters praising this Prairie Farm Assistance Act and asking that it be kept on the statute book, that it be enlarged or extended. The farmers ask that it should not be done away with because it is the only thing they have to help them. Have hon. members ever stopped to think that even with the small crop last year and the low grades, there is no relief in western Canada? Why? It is because these bonuses have been paid and have been evenly distributed among our farmers so that they are able to get by.
There are two schools of thought in western Canada with regard to this wheat question, and I shall deal with them in a moment.
I come now to the wheat acreage reduction plan. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act will cost the government something in the neighbourhood of $15,000,000. Under the wheat acreage reduction plan the government pays S4 per acre for each acre taken out of wheat and put into summer-fallow, and $2 per acre for every acre put into coarse grains. That will cost the government between $25,000,000 and $35,000,000. I understand that $25,000,000 has been paid out.

The only people who complain about this wheat acreage reduction plan are those who did not do what the government asked them to do. A lot of these people thought they knew better; they thought the price of wheat was going up and they put all their acreage into wheat. Because of the poor crop and the poor grades they suffered, when they received no wheat acreage reduction bonus they began to howl like stuck pigs. They are squealing because they think they should be getting something when they did not do what they were told to do. Those who went into coarse grains got the $2 per

Wheat Board Act

acre as well as the higher price for coarse grains. By doing what the government told them to do, they were much better off; they were able to get by.
We come to the next, the prairie farm income plan to pay the farmer for his increased cost of living. It is expected that this will cost between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000-I understand it will cost about
S16,000,000. If we take these three bonus plans together, $15,000,000 for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, $30,000,000 for the wheat acreage plan and $15,000,000 to $20,000,000 for the prairie farm income plan, we have a total in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000. We expect to market 200 million bushels of wheat, and if we do it will mean that we have received about 30 cents per bushel by way of bonuses on an acreage basis. So it can be said that we are getting a dollar a bushel for our wheat. It is only a question of how it is to be paid, on an acreage or on a bushelage basis. This government is paying 70 cents on a bushelage basis and 30 cents on an acreage basis. I have a farmer in my constituency who farms about two and one-half sections of land and he told me that he received $9 per bushel for his wheat. He produced 300 bushels of w'heat, and his wheat acreage reduction bonus, prairie farm assistance bonus and prairie farm income bonus amounted to $2,700. There are many farmers who received more than a dollar a bushel for their wheat; I can name hundreds of them. These are some of the things that the government has done this year for the wheat grower in western Canada.
I have spoken of what was done for the man who had wheat and what was done for the man who through climatic conditions had no wheat. I now come to the question of storage. We felt that we were not going to have enough storage, and so year by year we have been increasing our storage through the last few years. On January 1, 1939, our storage capacity was 422 million bushels; on January 1, 1940, it was 424 million bushels, and on January 1, 1941, 437 million bushels. Now, on January 1, 1942, we have a storage capacity of about 600 million bushels. Seeking to obtain this additional storage the government signed an agreement with the elevator companies that they would not decrease storage charges for two years. I am sorry that was ever done. I think it should not have been done. I think it was a mistake. I think that storage charges are too high, and they should be lowered. I shall deal with that more fully later. I wish to go on now to what is proposed for this year, because time is pressing.
The government proposes to take 280 million bushels of wheat this year, which is 50

million bushels more than the government proposed to take last year. How is it that the government expects to be able to take 50 million bushels more this year? First of all, as I have said, we have increased our storage capacity; we have more elevators. The second reason is that we are exporting more wheat. From August 1 to January 31, 1941-42, we exported 111 million bushels of wheat and flour; from August 1 to January 31, 1940-41, we exported 79 million bushels. The export for t'he whole world was 154 million bushels from August 1, 1941, to February 28, 1942. That is what we have done, and that is why the government is able to take more wheat this year.
We are also to have the quota system again this year. The next thing the government proposes is an initial price of 90 cents for wheat, instead of 70 cents, with participation certificates. That is an increase of 20 cents a bushel. It is a legitimate price, on Which I believe the farmer ought to be able to make a living. I shall deal with that more fully later. We have the Prairie Farm Assistance Act again this year. We have also the wheat acreage reduction bonus, which will net the farmer $2 an acre for coarse grains, the same as last year, and cost the government about $15,000,000, and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act will cost another $15,000,000. That is worth another 10 cents a bushel to the farmer. So that the farmer is getting this year 90 cents a bushel as an initial payment and 10 cents by way of bonus, or altogether $1 a bushel, calculated in a different way. That is what is proposed with respect to wheat for this year.
In setting a price of 90 cents a bushel the government does not set a ceiling on the price of wheat,. A ceiling has been or is likely to be set for flour and bread. I think that is one question that ought to be investigated. I remember that before this farm delegation came to Ottawa they held meetings throughout western Canada, and everywhere they went they pointed out that the price of bread was 7i to 8 cents a loaf when wheat was selling at $2.50; that it was the same price when wheat was selling at $1.50 a bushel, and that it was still between 7J and 8 cents with wheat at 70 cents a bushel. So they said there must be an Ethiopian in the wood-pile somewhere, and it is time we got him out. I think the whole question of the price of bread and flour as compared with the price of wheat should be investigated. The price control board and the wheat board ought to investigate this question together and decide what is a legitimate price for the milling of wheat and the baking of bread, and then a ceiling should be

Wheat Board Act
put on. bread and flour, the finished product, leaving the raw product, wheat, where it is at the present time.
I come now to another matter. There are two schools of thought in western Canada with regard to the wheat problem. One school of thought thinks that all the assistance that is given to the wheat growers of western Canada should be on an acreage basis. The other contends that all the assistance given to the wheat growers of western Canada should be on a bushelage basis. This delegation of four hundred that came to Ottawa were all of one mind, representing one school of thought. They said that the assistance should be all on a bushelage basis. We want dollar wheat, they said, knowing that that was a popular slogan. But I have received hundreds of letters from farmers in western Canada saying: If we are going to have dollar wheat, all right, but do not do away with the bonus. There are two schools of thought, as I say. Those who think that the assistance should be entirely on an acreage basis say that two-thirds of the wheat crop of 1940 was grown on about 22 million acres. The government has surveyed and tabulated all this information and knows how much each farmer has. These people say: If you are going to give the farmers who came to Ottawa one dollar a bushel, an increase of 30 cents a bushel from 70 cents, that amounts to $90,000,000 on 300 million bushels. And if you are going to give them $90,000,000, they say, the right and proper way is to give it at $4 an acre, for two-thirds of the 1940 wheat crop, to everyone, instead of as an increase of thirty cents a bushel on wheat. What is the good, they say, of an increased payment on wheat if you have no wheat? The kind of hailstorm we have in western Canada sweeps through a strip five miles wide and will go from ten to forty miles. The man in the centre of that area who is hailed out and so has no wheat will not get a cent, but the man on the outside edge who had rain and not hail will have a better crop than usual, perhaps twenty-five to thirty bushels to the acre. If you concede what the delegation wants you will allow thirty cents a bushel, which means that if a man has thirty bushels to the acre he gets $9; if forty, $12; but the man who has no crop will have to go to the prairie farm assistance people for a grant of no more than $2 or $2.50 an acre. They ask, is that just, is that equitable, is that fair? The man who has no crop may be just as good a farmer in just as good a district, but he is so unfortunate as to be hailed out. By distributing the money on a bushelage instead of an acreage 44561-76}
basis you will be requiring the man without a crop to live on $2.50 an acre, whereas the man with the big crop will receive $8 or $10 or more per acre to help him along. Dollar wheat is a first-class thing for the man who has thirty to forty bushels an acre and thirty to forty thousand bushels of wheat, but what is the good of it to the man who has no wheat? And the man who has no wheat, or a poor crop, is as much-and more-a charge of the government as the man who has a good crop; he should be and must be looked after.
These are some of the problems we have to contend1 with, some of the things which I am continuously being written about and asked to support. The government, however, this year has taken the middle course. It has given some increase in the price of wheat, from 70 cents up to 90 cents, and it is also maintaining the wheat acreage reduction plan, which farmers can participate in, and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for the benefit of those who have no crop. So that some of their assistance is given on an acreage basis and some on a bushelage basis; and as a compromise I am ready and. willing to support that. But I am one of those who favour the acreage basis rather than the bushelage basis, and I am not alone in that view. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle quoted Professor Hope a while ago. I, too, will quote from what the professor said, in regard to this. I refer to a statement in the national farm radio forum, prairie regional broadcast, on Monday, January 12. Speaking at that time, the professor said:
I feel that the additional money required to raise the western farm income to a reasonable basis will be better spent on additional acreage bonuses rather than by raising the price per bushel of wheat.
There are some who say, "We do not want charity; we want the price of wheat raised. We do not want these bonuses; they are charity." I may be dense, but I cannot see the difference. If the government is going to raise the price of wheat to ninety cents the money will come out of the treasury, and whether the farmer receives it as a bonus added to the price of wheat or in the form of a grant at so much per acre, it is all the same. If one is charity, so is the other.
I regretted the reference of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) to what he called parity price. If you are going to speak of parity prices I would only point out this. If you take the price of labour in 1913-14 and compare it with what it is now, you find that labour received about 154 in 1938 where it got 100 in 1914. Without a doubt, agricultural

products, especially wheat, are away below the parity price as it was in 1913-14. But so is the return on capital. Make no mistake about that. You know just as well as I do the difference between the present time and the last war. The first loan, in 1915, for $100,000,000, bore five per cent interest; the next in 1916, another $100,000,000, was also at five per cent interest; in 1917, $139,000,000, five per cent interest. The first victory loan, $398,000,000, yielded five and a half per cent; so also did the loan of 8660,000,000 in 1918. All the three loans in 1917 and 1918 were tax free. That term cannot be applied to the loans of 1915 and 1916 because at that time we did not have any income tax. The United States began it in 1914, three years before they went into the war, but ours was not put on until 1917.
Another point should be borne in mind in this connection. If we are going to establish this parity for the farmer, capital too will want to be put on a parity. They are wide awake and looking after their interests. What about the mortgages in western Canada? What did we pay at the time of the last war? Eight and nine per cent; in some cases ten per cent. Now the rate is cut to five and six per cent. Do you want to go back to eight, nine and ten per cent? I do not think so. What we should ask for is a reasonable price rather than a parity price. I draw that to the attention of the house because I believe it is important.
I come now to the question of storage. In July, 1940, the rate for wheat storage was one-thirtieth of a cent a day. At that time the Liberal members from western Canada met and discussed the question, and we sent in a presentation to the grain commission asking that the rate be reduced. As a result it was reduced to one forty-fifth of a cent per day. As confirmation of that statement I have in my hand a press report which went out on July 28, 1940, from the chief commissioner of the Board, of Grain Commissioners for Canada. I refer to it because my statement on this matter has been disputed on the platform. The wheat pool has taken credit for this having been reduced. I quote from the press release of the board:
The annual tariff meeting of the Board of Grain Commissioners was held at Winnipeg on July 9th, when the board received submissions from the Northwest Grain Dealers' Association, Terminal Association, Saskatchewan Pool Elevators, and the Manitoba Pool Elevators, and also advanced the submission of tile Alberta Pool Elevators.
. Listen to what he says:
These submissions dealt with the maintenance of the current tariff rates.

The submissions dealt with the present rate which is one-thirtieth of a cent. He goes on:
Submissions were also received from certain western members of parliament in favour of reducing tariffs in the national interest.
He does not say anything about receiving submissions from any other elevator companies or line companies, but as a result of these submissions made to the grain commission they did reduce the carrying charges or storage charges on wheat from one thirtieth to one forty-fifth of a cent. For that reason I maintain that we western members are entitled to a certain amount of credit for it. In my opinion the charge of one-thirtieth of a cent may have been all right when our elevators were quite full for one month in the year aiid then half full for three or four months and empty the rest of the year; but now that the elevators are filled to the roof twelve months of the year one forty-fifth of a cent is too much. I suggest that it is time our grain handling charges were overhauled. I think they should be reduced. They should be cut in half. I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.

The rule is clear that no member may anticipate a discussion which may come before the house at a later date. I would not insist upon the observance of that rule in this case, because of the fact that the house has already adopted a resolution giving precedence to government business, and for that reason the resolution of the hon, member might not be reached this session. He has, in a measure, discussed it on his amendment which is now before the house. I would suggest, however, that having discussed it now, his motion should be withdrawn from the order paper.
With regard to the amendment itself, I think the rule is perfectly clear. The recommendation of the crown required for the imposition of charges upon the taxpayer is compulsory on committee as well as on the house itself. There is no exception. The inclusion in a bill of a provision authorizing the payment of public money is nothing but a statutory appropriation w'hich can be made only upon the crown's recommendation and in committee of the whole house, under the provision of section 54 of the British North America Act.
It is hardly necessary to quote any authorities in support of such a clear declaration of the constitution of Canada. The principle therein set forth is one of the fundamental tenets of British parliamentary law, and it is observed in the United Kingdom as well as in all the dominion parliaments. Sir Erskine May's book entitled "Parliamentary Practice", 13th edition, says, at page 505:
If any motion, or bill, or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the house or in a committee, which requires but fails to receive the recommendation of the crown, it is the duty of the chair to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion, or to direct the withdrawal of the bill.
Paragraph (b) of the hon. member's amendment asks for the establishment in every constituency in Canada of exemption tribunals, whose object would be to examine particularly all! requests which might be presented before such tribunals by farmers' sons. It therefore falls under the rule I have stated, and I rule the amendment out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure there will be widespread disappointment throughout western Canada as a result of the policy announced by the government yesterday for the disposal of the 1942-43 wheat crop. The people of western Canada had reason to feel in the past few months that a new deal was about to come into existence for agriculture. The visit of the farm delegation to Ottawa, the excellent press notices the delegation had and the sympathetic reception they received from cabinet council all gave the people of western Canada reason to feel that probably we were on the verge of a new deal for that part of the country. I am afraid there will be a feeling now that instead of a new deal we have received a dirty deal.
When I say that, of course I am not unmindful of the commendable features of the legislation. For some months back, hon. members on this side of the house, particularly the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) have been asking the government to put a floor under coarse grains, realizing that if we were to attempt to encourage the fanner to leave wheat production and go into the production of coarse grains, we could do so only by putting a floor under them. That is one of the commendable features of the legislation brought down yesterday.
But my main objection to the legislation is that the government is following its old policy of beating a sort of strategic retreat, like an army which holds a position until it is no longer tenable, and then when it is almost surrounded, makes a retreat to the .next position it believes it can hold. It clings to that position as long as possible, and then makes another retreat. We have had that procedure now for five or six years-a series of strategic retreats rather than brilliant offensives.

It may be a retreat forward, but It has required a great deal of pressure to get any movement at all. I ask the house to take a glimpse at what has happened. In 1935, after long years of clamouring for it, the farmers were given a wheat board, a payment of 87i cents a bushel, and participation certificates. In 1936 this government was in office; the 87J cents was cut to 80 cents, and a new personnel was appointed to the wheat board. In 1937 an order in council was passed stating that
farmers could not deliver their wheat to the wheat board, even if they wanted to, as long as the market price of wheat was above 90 cents. The same situation obtained in 1938.
Then in 1939 two bills were brought down, and we thought again we were getting some general improvement for agriculture. The first of those two bills was the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. At this point let me say just a word about that legislation. The hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) has taken to himself, and the party with which he is associated, the credit for supporting that piece of legislation. He intimated that nobody else wanted it, and that no one else was in favour of it. That suggestion of course is absolutely inaccurate. For a great many years before it was brought down, not only members of the group with which I am associated, but I should think members of almost all groups in the house were asking for some type of crop insurance. As a matter of fact, the previous year a resolution had been passed unanimously by the house endorsing the principle of crop insurance for farmers. Therefore, when the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was introduced it was acceptable to all parts of the house. But it was brought down in conjunction with legislation which was to provide an advance or cash payment of 60 cents a bushel. Those hon. members who were in the house at the time will remember the long struggle which took place not only here in the house but in western Canada. The result was that the minister withdrew the bill, substituting for it a new one raising the initial price to 70 cents. It will be recalled that again in 1940 we received an initial price of 70 cents.
By that time the war was upon us, and there was a feeling that the price ought to be higher, and that wheat had become a more valuable commodity. I would remind the house, for instance, of the speech made with respect to the price of wheat by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) during the election of 1940. I quote from the Regina Leader Post of March 12, 1940, an article headed "Gardiner talks wheat, correcting Manion mistakes". It reads as follows:
Wheat could all be sold to Britain to-morrow at not less than 87 cents a bushel. If it were, the farmer could now obtain at least ten cents a bushel on his participation certificates.

While it would thus remain where it is it would be entirely out of the hands of the farmers. We believe that Britain will pay us more for our wheat when she is ready to take it.

They asked for an initial payment of $1 a bushel; they asked that stocks of wheat represented by the carryover should be taken off the market and held as a national emergency war reserve; they asked that from August 1, 1941, all sales of wheat should be credited to the crop year 1941-42, and they asked that the crop year 1941-42 should be declared an emergency year under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act irrespective of the market prices prevailing. As a result of these meetings and as a result of their failure to get any adequate response to their representations from the government, a delegation came to Ottawa. In the first place, for the wheat consumed in Canada there is no reason for the treasury to pay it. We have cheap wheat in this country. The milling industry and the baking industry can afford to pay a price for wheat which is on a parity basis. They have paid it before. Back in the fall of 1938 the price of wheat went over $1.40, and there was no complaint. They can afford to pay a reasonable price for wheat to be milled in Canada. Second, the only other place where we sell wheat is the United Kingdom. As to the wheat we are giving to the United Kingdom-because it will probably come within the gift of $1,000 million worth of products which we shall be making to Great Britain-I think western Canada is justified when it says that if we are going to make a gift to Great Britain of so many million bushels of wheat, that is a gift which ought to be paid for by all the people rather than by the small section who grow it. That is why it would not have been unreasonable to expect the government to have paid a dollar as this initial price.
Another thing is that no step has been taken yet, and there is no indication that a step will be taken, to remove the surplus from the market and save it as an emergency. There should be an emergency reserve. It has been said over and over again that when this war is over, food will be a weapon to reestablish peace; it will be an implement of reconstruction. All right; then Canada as a whole ought to pay for that weapon. We do not ask the people of Ontario, or the manufacturers, to make tanks for nothing as a weapon to win the war. Then there is no reason why we should ask the farmers to pay for a weapon to win the peace. If we are going to use wheat as a weapon to reconstruct the world, it ought to be paid for by the whole Canadian people rather than by the wheat producers of western Canada. We would welcome from the government some statement that the sales in this next crop year will be applied to that year's wheat, because if we do that, and if the wheat is sold for more than the initial price, instead of the extra money being eaten up in interest and storage charges there will be some chance of it going back to the producer, who certainly has a right to expect whatever remuneration is coming.

If the principle which we accept is that of depressed prices for agriculture, we shall impose on western Canada from now to the end of the war a standard of living which will mean poverty and insecurity for our people.

depressed area, from which the more aggressive members of society will be fleeing, and where we shall have people living who stay there only because they are too poor to move out. I have no hesitation in saying from my place in this House of Commons that the price should have been at least $1. Why all this niggardliness toward a great section of this Canadian nation? For the want of a dime, a ten cent piece, we are raising a question in the minds of the people of western Canada. Wheat has been a casualty long enough. Surely the time has come when we should take it out of the casualty list and place it in the front line so that it can go forward fighting for what we are all fighting for to-day-democracy. I appreciate fully the assistance that was given to the western farmers to help them in those days when it was difficult to find a sale for their products, when there were such large stocks of wheat for which markets could not be found. The measures now before the house do not go far enough to meet the situation that now prevails,
Wheat Board Act

The present price of 70 cents, a 'bushel, No. 1 northern, Fort William or Vancouver, gives the farmer a maximum gross return of approximately 50 cents a bushel at his shipping point. The proposed price of 90 cents a bushel will mean that the farmer will get approximately 70 cents a bushel at 'his shipping point. There can be no debate that with present costs, with general expenses and living expenses being what they are, a return of 50 cents a bushel, or even 70 cents a bushel is not enough, even if we have a bumper crop in Saskatchewan.
The Monetary Times of August, 1930, contained a survey of the cost of producing wheat, and it was shown that it cost 84J cents to raise a bushel of western wheat. The United Farmers of Manitoba carried out an investigation in 1933, and even with all the paring that they could do they could not get the cost of production below 78 cents a bushel. Professor Hope of the university of Saskatchewan has been quoted in this house on many occasions, and we have had other opinions as to the actual cost of raising a bushel of wheat. All these figures compare favourably with the average United States cost of production.
Dollar wheat would give the prairie farmer 80 cents at his shipping point, and I submit that that is little enough for the sacrifices he has endured over a long period of time and the contribution he has made, not only to the economic structure of Canada but to the whole world. There is no wheat raised anywhere else in the world quite like the wheat that we raise on the western prairies. A loaf of bread produced from Canadian wheat will contain 3,000 cubic centimeters; a loaf produced from the same amount of Australian wheat will contain 2,180 cubic centimeters, and a loaf produced from English wheat, 1,830 cubic centimeters. A loaf of bread produced from Canadian wheat stands far above the bread produced from wheat raised in Germany, France or Italy.
The domestic economy of western Canada is based upon our wheat economy, and in the main this cannot be changed. The agricultural authorities are thoroughly familiar with the factors of soil, water and climate. The Minister of Agriculture, speaking in this house on his bill, proved to the members that we had this wheat triangle. Speaking before the Canadian chamber of commerce in convention in Regina in 1931, John W. Dafoe, editor of the Winnipeg Free Press and coeditor of the Sirois report, a man who for forty years has followed the difficult economy of western Canada and who knows the situation of the prairies perhaps better than any

other living man because he has made a special study of all phases and angles, had this to say:
Check over the situation any way you like and you will come hack to this: that we have in western Canada at least 12 million acres that will have to be abandoned if not put to wheat raising, for which, under modern conditions of power farming and rapidly maturing kinds of wheat, they are highly suited.
There are about 290,000 farms in the prairie provinces. If we take an average of four persons to a farm, that means that 1,160,000 western Canadians are dependent upon farm income. In Saskatchewan whence I come, which can grow enough wheat in one year to feed all the people of Canada for five years, or all the people of Saskatchewan for fifty years, about 76 per cent of the farm income is from wheat, and that is one of the reasons why we who represent Saskatchewan constituencies-whether it be town or city makes no difference-are so much interested in the wheat economy of that province. Because of the low prices which have prevailed for the last number of years the farmers of western Canada have suffered. But low prices have beeh one handicap only. Those farmers have suffered crop failure after crop failure due to circumstances over which they had no control. They have suffered from rust; they have suffered from drought; they have suffered from grasshoppers and from frost, and because of all these things they find themselves in the position they are now in.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I know the situation in a great many of the rural areas of Saskatchewan as well as any other member. In the practice of my profession of medicine I have spent many years in the constituency of Humboldt, in its rural areas. I have met the people in their humble homes, and I know the hardships they have had to endure. They are a proud people. They did not want hand-outs from the government and they did not ask for them. They tried to keep body and soul together before any governmental assistance came to them in the days now past when we had1 our relief problems on those plains and prairies. The majority of our prairie farmers live in a most meagre way. They have no elaborate homes, no high-class furnishings. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) the other night gave certain statistics in connection with the modernized homes that we have in the prairie provinces. The children of our farmers receive only a very limited education. Our people have gone through all the handicaps and the hardships I have mentioned and, now, what do they find? They see prosperity

Wheat Board Act
coming to the great industrial areas of Ontario, and I cannot understand how any government can afford to be niggardly in dealing with the type of men and women who have given the best years of their life to carving from out that wilderness of western Canada homes for themselves and their children.
We see in our mind's eye to-night that humble father and mother sitting alone in their prairie home, trying to keep the old farm going, with all the difficulties that go with it-all that they owe on farm mortgage, high interest rates, low prices for their products, and all the other things which have befallen them as I mentioned a few moments ago. They may be thinking of their son, and1, Mr.	Speaker,	this	touches many	inSaskatchewan. That son may be the boy you read about in the western Canadian newspapers, that boy from Saskatchewan who was shot	down over Singapore or	in	theLibyan desert or in one of the commando raids on France or Norway or over the English channel. Should we treat these people in a different way from the people of other parts of Canada? By this wheat legislation we are proposing to jeopardize not only the future of western Canada	but	the ability	of	itspeople to	help win	this	war-and	all	for
what? All for the want of a ten-cent piece as an initial payment.
