subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows all about it, so after I hear him make his speech I may change my views. After all, I am not tied up as he is to some fantastic theories of money or something like that.
In the Atlantic charter it was pointed out that the great new order would provide freedom from fear and freedom from want in those countries which have been overrun by the enemy. Surely we can do little less than to start this great new order here in Canada by seeing to it that the people on the western plains shall become free from fear and free from want.
Wage and salaried workers in Canada are now given protection to meet the increased costs of living. The farmers who are able to engage in mixed farming practices are protected under governmental policy and receive adequate compensation for the production of
live stock and dairy products. The sharply improved price of coarse grains arising from the government's policy of promoting the production of live stock and dairy products materially aids those who can successfully engage in this particular phase of farming activity.
But what about the wheat farmer, the farmer in that triangle which the Minister of Agriculture drew yesterday? In that broadcast which I mentioned in the opening part of my remarks the Prime Minister said:
Agriculture itself is a national asset which must be preserved.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether wheat farming is not a substantial part of Canada's agriculture. I ask you further, whether or not 90 cent wheat will preserve that part of our agriculture. It can be proved that 90-cent wheat is not adequate-absolutely	not
adequate.
Let me examine briefly the existing price set-up for our prairie wheat and compare it with prices of other grains.
A few months ago the Canadian wheat board, acting as administrator on behalf of the wartime prices and trade board, issued an order fixing the maximum price at which Ontario wheat might be sold in eastern Canada at SI.26 a bushel, basis delivered at Montreal. This was the highest price at which wheat was sold in the basic period between September 15 and October 11, 1941. Last January the Northwest Line ellevators' association which, as is well known to those of us who come from the farming section of western Canada, is vitally interested in the welfare of a vast number of western farmers in that area, approached the wartime prices and trade board for an adjustment of western wheat prices. The association said:
In view of the action already taken by your board in respect to Ontario wheat, and having regard to the superior milling value of western spring wheat, we feel that the ceiling price of wheat for all Canada should be not less than the price of $1.26 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern delivered Montreal. This would make the ceiling price at Fort William and Vancouver a minimum of approximately $1.15 per bushel.
I do not like that word "ceiling" in the submission of the association, but I like its appraisal of the problem being faced by the west and I like its energy in trying to get something done for our western agriculturists. It asked for wheat at $1.15 a bushel. The organized wheat growers asked only for $1 wheat as an initial payment.
We are not asking that this be based on the price of wheat and other essential farm commodities in 1913-14 or the years just prior to the outbreak of the first world war, although that is widely accepted as a fair basis. The
Wheat Board Act

government of the United States has taken the price relationship existing between 1909 and 1914 as a proper base for stabilizing current farm income, and there is little difference between the 1909-1914 and the 19131914 bases. The Searle Grain company in its valuable index, which has been quoted many times in this chamber, shows that the 1913 price of No. 1 northern wheat, basis Fort William, was 87J cents a bushel, and the cost of the essential commodities which the farmer has to buy has increased fifty per cent since that time. Therefore, to place the farmer in the same position comparatively as he enjoyed in 1913-14, the price should be increased fifty per cent. But the organized farmers of western Canada are asking only $1 a bushel as the initial payment for their wheat. I know some will raise objections to this. Some will say that to do so will increase our surpluses and that you should stop growing wheat; others will say that it is too expensive.
Let us explore briefly these two objections. Take the question of surpluses. We find on every hand that what we have is not surpluses, but scarcities." One of our great difficulties in the present war is that, so far from having surpluses, there has been a scarcity of every commodity, excepting wheat, which we have required to help win this war, and the only people who were prepared to face the issues of the world war in which we are engaged to-day were the prairie farmers of western Canada. We can certainly thank our lucky stars that we have these surpluses. It is only three years since, having carried a burdensome surplus of wheat for some years, we had to scrape our wheat bins clean, following the poor crops of 1936 and 1937. Recurrence of such a situation would be most serious. If we were now short of wheat, the government would go to any lengths-there would be no question of cost-to get the farmers of western Canada back into full production of wheat.
Surely it can be readily appreciated that food, and particularly wheat, is as important a war requirement as are munitions. Wheat can be stored for longer periods of time and at less expense than any other foodstuffs. The need for maintaining substantial reserves of wheat as an essential requirement of the war and the subsequent peace negotiations is certainly recognized.
Indeed, the need for food reserves is more than ever apparent, because increasingly large wheat and agricultural areas are being laid waste by war. Accepting wheat as necessary to winning the war, and necessary to win the peace, the government must be prepared to pay the farmer a reasonable price for pro-

ducing wheat. It pays necessary prices-whatever the price the manufacturer wants-for munitions of war. Is wheat any less important for the winning of this war than those other essentials of which we speak in connection with our war activity? Surely I do not need to reiterate the urgency for the united nations to maintain ample reserves of food as an essential requirement of the war and the peace which will follow. In this connection the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of Great Britain, speaking on August 20, 1940, said:
We shall do our best to encourage the building up of reserves of food all over the world so that there will always be held before the eyes of the people of Europe, including the Germans, the certainty that the shattering of nazi power would bring to them all immediate food, freedom and peace.
The Prime Minister of Canada in his radio address which I have mentioned twice before, said:
Wheat held in reserve constitutes an invaluable war asset.
!Need we, then, be fearful that giving the western farmer dollar wheat would build up our stocks too much? Not in the least, even if we had a bumper crop on the prairies this coming season, and nobody believes that we shall have, because moisture conditions all over western Canada were never worse than this year, owing to the light snowfall this past winter. Western Canada may have a crop failure just as complete as that of 1937. But even if we should have 500 million bushels as a steady reserve, we would not be too prudent. With the armies of Germany and Russia steadily moving back and forth in those great areas of Russia which have been destroyed, areas which will not be able to go back into wheat production, the day may come when we shall suddenly be asked to feed our great ally, Russia, that has been of such immense assistance to us in this present struggle.
Wre do not need to worry about surpluses because the government is protecting itself against surpluses. The farmers will not grow a surplus of wheat because the government says that the restricted deliveries will be only 2S0 million bushels. It is impossible, of course, to estimate accurately what the crop will be in 1942. But in my opinion, and in the opinion of others who are interested in the grain trade, the figures which the minister gave yesterday were the outside figures. It is our opinion that dollar wheat would not in any way embarrass the wheat board, and the government has amply protected itself by putting in the clause providing for a delivery quota of 280 million bushels.

Wheat Board Act
As to the price, let us suppose that the deliveries will be 280 millioa bushels. Let us suppose that the farmers do turn over that much wheat, to the wheat board, and let us suppose further that all that wheat comes from the prairie provinces. Ten cents a bushel, providing for dollar wheat instead of ninety cent wheat, would cost approximately $28 million. We talk to-day in such large figures that they are absolutely unintelligible to the ordinary man on the street. I think the expression has been coined that they are "astronomical". They have become so large that one is unable to comprehend them. But we shall be spending in this fiscal year nearly $3,000 million. One can go into the argument of percentage, but it is useless, because by comparison the amount which would be taken out of the public treasury would be so small that it would be only the proverbial drop in the proverbial bucket compared with the great sums which we are expending in every direction.
There is one thing that we should keep in mind. While we are talking about what this war is going to cost, we are liable to lose the war if we lose sight of the importance of certain things-for instance, if we quarrel over a little sum of $28 million which would keep up the morale of western Canada. Would we not spend $28 million to keep up the morale of India? This dollar wheat has become almost a byword on the plains and prairies of the province that I represent in this house, and this money would not be frozen. It would immediately go back into circulation in the form of war savings stamps, war savings certificates, payments to merchants and doctors and scores of creditors whom the farmers have to pay. I have found in the farming community which I represent that nothing gives the people greater pleasure than to be able to take a little bit of money and go and pay off some of their old indebtedness. This $28 million that would be handed to the people of the prairie provinces would help them to do this, and the money would not all stay in Saskatchewan; it would find its way, as such money has always done in the past, to eastern Canada.
I am sure that the people in other parts of the dominion will sympathize with the submission that was made to the Prime Minister and his government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. So often we hear it said, "Oh, the people of Ontario or Quebec or the maritimes would not stand for it, or it could not be put through the House of Commons." I doubt very much that that represents the attitude of the people of those provinces, and I say that from my association with members from
Ontario and from other parts of the country. I believe they are quite fair-minded and will look upon this situation in the same light as we do. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is an organization representing the organized farmers from all parts of the dominion, and I quote the following from their submission:
All of the member bodies of this federation from western Canada are on record to the effect that the basic price for the coming year should be not less than $1 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern at lakehead or seaboard terminals. We can assure the government that opinion in Manitoba and Alberta is equally strong, and that such a request has also the support of the agricultural interests in other parts of Canada represented by this federation.
The prairie farmers are not asking for anything that is beyond the reach of this government; they are not asking for anything that is going to ruin the federal treasury. They realize as well as anyone else that the government have a tough job and that our farmers and the rural population of the country are straining every effort to ensure victory and peace to the allied nations of the world. They are also committed to action which will help in every way. There is nothing they have not done to try to bring this abouQ including a change in the method of farming. To the best of their ability they have tried changing from wheat raising to the raising of pork products. Everything within their power they have done to help to win the war and to assist the government.
Let me ask you this, Mr. Speaker: Who can estimate the upsurge of feeling that would go all through the west as a result of news that there would be dollar wheat. Suppose such news went out from this parliament; can you imagine the psychological effect it would have on those poor downtrodden people who have suffered so much? It would act upon the blood of those farmers like a tonic. But 90-cent wheat! Why all this niggardliness?-because that is the only term I can think of. Now is the great opportunity for this government. The cost would be but little more than the new price, and there would be no danger of the accumulation of new surpluses. Moreover, judging from the figures of cost of wheat production, dollar wheat would be no more than is fair.
1 hope this government will reconsider the matter. I hope they will give every consideration to the representations made by the great delegation that came here. It was not an ordinary delegation; it was not like so many delegations that come here and present cases to the government of Canada, setting forth the maximum amount that they would like to get, in the expectation of getting perhaps
Wheat Board Act

half of that amount, in which event they are well pleased. This was a different delegation. It represented all phases of thought in Saskatchewan, all phases of activity-farmers, business men, professional men and merchants. These were reasonable men, and they took the attitude that since this country was in the throes of the greatest war known to history, they would not ask for anything that was unreasonable. They asked for the minimum amount, and I have every hope that, with that keen sense of appreciation which the Prime Minister has of our agricultural problems, with that persuasive ability that characterizes the Minister of Agriculture, these two men will be able to convince the other members of the federal government, who are opposed to giving a dollar as the initial payment to the farmers of western Canada, of the wisdom of such a step.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
shall be supporting the amendment which was moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). Had it not been moved I would have moved a similar amendment in speaking this evening. The idea embodied in that amendment is not new to this house. My colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), speaking on April 8, 1941, said, as reported at page 2280 of Hansard:
I have risen to move an amendment based on the condition of agriculture. I think it will be agreed by all hon. members that in time of war the morale of this nation cannot be as it should be if agriculture is pauperized. Agriculture taken as a whole in Canada is in a lamentable condition, and it is an anomalous condition of affairs that Canada, a great producer of food, should, in a world which sooner or later will require foodstuffs, try to find means to bring about a reduction in the production of wheat. I move therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Peel:
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
It be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make.

speechtext:
I am not sure how several members to whom we listened yesterday and to-day voted at that time. They probably voted against it.
We have listened to other speakers agitating for a higher price, including the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who was

very much heated in his argument yesterday evening, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). They inserted some provisos, however, as to the manner in which they were bound to the great Liberal party and why they must follow it at all costs to the country.
I am sure many people in western Canada will be very much disappointed with this bill, for several reasons. Not only will they be disappointed in regard to the price, but they expected that this policy would be announced earlier in the year. One month ago to-day, on February 10, in this very chamber I expressed the hope that the two ministers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would soon announce the wheat policy for this year. I pointed out that in previous years a good deal of this policy had been carried out by order in council, and the Minister of Agriculture interrupted to say that this year we must wait until the speech from the throne was disposed of because it would be all covered by legislation. Despite that statement by the minister, however, we were told yesterday that some part of the policy still will be implemented by order in council. I was one of those who, a year ago, greatly criticized this practice of passing orders in council, and I think I was right in so doing. This afternoon, in regard to the wheat acreage reduction scheme, an order in council concerning summer-fallow, which was passed on November 27, 1941, was quoted. I need not read the entire preamble, but the order in council provides:
"Summer-fallow" means the cultivation or management of fallow land in such a way as to conserve soil moisture or to prevent soil drifting, or both.
That was passed on November 27, 1941, with relation to the management of the scheme during the previous summer. Another order in council was passed on November 21, 1941, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with respect to the handling of wheat. So I think we should realize how necessary it is that these policies should be introduced by means of legislation.
Yesterday I listened very attentively to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the wheat situation, and the announcement of the 90-cent price for the 1942 crop. Then we had the statement by the Minister of Agriculture as to wheat acreage reduction, the demand for feed grain, animal products and other agricultural commodities for the war effort. I should like to compliment the minister upon his statement. I do not agree with everything he said, but he had

Wheat Board Act
a big job to do and I think he is to be complimented upon the way he did it. Then, following those statements, we listened to the impassioned arguments put forward by the hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Rosthern to which I have already referred. They coupled with their arguments, however, the statement that they were bound to the Liberal party and must follow that party at all costs. I have been rather convinced in recent weeks that this delegation of some four hundred pool farmers, dirt farmers from western Canada, probably impressed this government to a greater extent with regard to the difficulties of the western farmer than their representatives in the Liberal party have been able to do for the past six or seven years. I remember that in 1934 the present Minister of Agriculture led the Liberal party of Saskatchewan into power in that province. During the course of that campaign, in the month of June, he had distributed throughout the province a handbill promising dollar wheat. I do not know why dollar wheat is always the great issue in a Saskatchewan election, but in any event this handbill, put out by authority of the Saskatchewan Liberal Association, said:
Trade will bring dollar wheat. Dollar wheat wilt end your troubles. Dollar wheat will run your farm and pay your taxes. Dollar wheat will pay the hired help and pay your repair bill. Dollar wheat will pay your insurance and buy your wife a new dress. Vote Liberal.
My recollection is that the people of that province voted Liberal; but, as the hon. member for Rosthern pointed out last night, the debts of the people have been accumulating year by year. He did not make 1934 the jump-off date, but he did give the figures for several years since then. On May 15, 1934, May wheat was quoted at 70J cents at Winnipeg and 86 cents at Chicago, and I think everyone will agree that the cost of production and the cost of living were not nearly as high then as they are to-day. I might give a comparison of the prices of some of the
necessary farm implements, as between 1934 and 1941:
1934	1941
Two-furrow gang plough	$137	50	$155	00Eight-foot cultivator	
143	00	162	50Twenty-row double disc drill 250	50	295	25Eight-foot binder	
257	00	327	00
The average increase in these four farm implements, which are most necessary on any farm, was 18i per cent during that period. Many hon. members know of the demand for power equipment to-day. In the Winnipeg Tribune of February 26 I ran across a short article making a comparison between army
tools and agricultural tools, by Mr. Q. H. Martinson, who said:
The army tools of to-day dwarf those of 1918, just as the machinery of present day agriculture has outmoded that of twenty-five years ago. Mechanized equipment to equip a half-section farm to-day in some instances costs as much as fifty per cent more than the horse-drawn equipment needed for the farm during the last war. During the last war farmers used a horse-drawn binder; to-day he uses a combine. He hauled his grain to town with team and wagon; to-day he uses motor trucks. He ploughed with a horse-drawm two-furrowed gang plough; to-day he uses a four-farrowed gang plough drawn by a fast moving tractor. Mechanized equipment for modern agriculture is now a prime and urgent necessity.
I remember that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) who, I believe, is also a member of the wheat committee of the cabinet, spoke in Souris in 1937. He stated then that if the west could produce a good crop of wheat, all the difficulties of the farmers would be solved. Well, we have produced a couple of good crops in Manitoba since then, but I am afraid our farmers are still facing many serious difficulties, especially in the matter of debt adjustment.
The great disparity between industry, organized labour and the wheat producer has been increasing continuously. The Searle market feature of January 7, 1942, contains an article on the financial reward to wheat producers and to industrial labour, taking the period 1913-14 as the parity basis. They point out that the price of wheat now should be $1 at the average country point for No. 1 northern wheat, w'hich would be equivalent to $1.20 for No. 1 northern at Fort William. Then they go on:
. . . because the cost of the things farmers have to buy, according to the Searle index, has increased 50-8 per cent since 1913-14. But the price of wheat to-day is actually only 53 cents. Therefore the price of wheat to-day is 45 per cent below "parity", or we can say that a bushel of wheat to-day has a purchasing power of 45 per cent less than it had in 1913-14.
For the industrial worker's average hourly rate of wages, however, to have the same purchasing power as it had in 1913-14, when it was at an index number of 100, it should now be at an index number of 145 (because the cost of living for industrial labour has gone up by 45 per cent since 1913-14). But the chart shows that the average hourly rate of wages to industrial labour is actually now at 210. Therefore the average hourly rate of wages to-day is 44 per cent higher than it was in 1913-14, or we can say that an hour of industrial labour now has a purchasing power of 44 per cent more than it had in 1913-14, or is 44 per cent higher than "parity".
The wide difference in the reward paid to wheat growers and to industrial labour respectively, should be borne in mind when proposals are considered to increase the price of wheat
Wheat Board Act

to its "parity" price of $1 a bushel to the farmer at his country point, for this chart reveals that even though wheat growers should receive $1 for their wheat, industrial labour would still be receiving a much higher relative return for their labour than wheat growers would he receiving for their wheat.
The period used by the government as a basis for parity with regard to industry and organized labour during this war is that of 1926 to 1929, rather than 1913-14. On that basis of parity wheat would be worth 81.42; oats, 60 cents; barley 71 cents, and rye, approximately $1. As stated yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture, the ceiling price for oats has been placed at 51-5 cents, or approximately 9 cents under parity. The price for barley has been placed at 64-8 cents, or 7 cents under parity. There had been a ceiling of approximately 66 cents on rye, which is 34 cents under parity. There is now a floor under oats placed at 45 cents, and under barley at 60 cents.
I now turn to a press dispatch appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 2. This article is written by Grant Dexter, many of whose articles have not been critical of the government. The article is headed "Increase in sale of goods and services in urban areas", and is as follows-
The rise is more marked in eastern Canada than in the prairie provinces. The increase from December, 1940, to December, 1941, varies from a peak of 21-5 per cent in Quebec to an actual loss of -2 per cent in southern Saskatchewan, 8-2 in all of Saskatchewan and 14-8 throughout rural Manitoba.
This is marked evidence of the purchasing power created in this country during war time, of which I expect to say more at another time.
May I at this point make some reference to voluntary enlistments by provinces. This matter has a direct bearing on the subject of wheat. I heard one hon. member go much further last night when referring to manufacturing. By way of proving that people in western Canada are doing their share in the war, I should like to give some percentages based on a return showing enlistments at December 31, 1941. These are voluntary enlistments for the active army, air force and navy, and are based on the 1931 population:

That is conclusive proof that these people who are labouring under such great handicaps, these western farmers, are doing their share, and that their sons and young people have done their bit by way of voluntary enlistment toward defending the nation.
Aside from food producing activities, the farmer has an important mission to fulfil. We need thriving agriculture for sociological reasons. Nations must never forget that agriculture's most valuable crop is the men and women who live by it. The resourcefulness, the self-reliance and the reserve of character that spring from working with nature and understanding her, from making decisions, from building on each separate farm a whole system of management of the soil out of the peculiar conditions that exist there, are moral assets we cannot lose without becoming incomparably poorer. I think that fact was brought out yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture when he drew the line from Morden to Saskatoon, and across to Lloydminster and down to Calgary, and pointed out that that area was chiefly and, in some cases, only fitted for the production of wheat, and that in that area provision had to be made for at least a million people. That is a factor which we as human beings cannot overlook, or lightly set aside.
Mr. G. Goddard Watts, in an article headed "An agricultural policy for Britain," points out that we need a countryside peopled by fresh rural communities in order to maintain the physical quality of our human stock. It is a tradition that three generations away from the soil will exhaust the vitality of a family, and that for refreshment and revitalization that family must leave its urban surroundings and reestablish itself in rural life. The nation which strangles its agriculture is on the way out. That is the verdict of history. I believe that in that statement there is plenty of food for thought for parliament at this time.
I have been somewhat disappointed that there has not been greater cooperation between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce and producers' organizations with respect to wheat. I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Tribune an article bearing out this thought. This was written by Mr. Q. H. Martinson; it is dated March 6, 1942, and reads as follows:
To-day the farmer and technical agriculturist are cooperating wholeheartedly with one purpose in view-the improvement of Canadian agriculture. To-day the producer and technical agriculturist are stressing the need for a permanent agricultural policy with little apparent response from the dominion government, apart from the work carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. However, the scope of the P.F.R.A. is restricted to only part of western

Wheat Board Act
Canada. Producers, producer organizations, technical agriculturists and other groups directly or indirectly associated with agriculture, fully realize the urgent necessity for the establishment of a long-term agricultural programme for Canada.
On July 12 last, a meeting of Manitoba members of C.S.T.A. was held at Brandon. At that meeting, a resolution urged the establishment of an advisory committee of agriculturists, farmer representatives, and others to advise the government on its wheat policy. Those presenting the resolution suggested that the government should make contact with all competent authorities and give careful consideration to suggestions and recommendations in the formation of an advisory committee. Specific recommendations entirely divorced from political considerations could then be offered the government. Despite the requests and advice of these recognized agricultural experts, the dominion government has failed to name an advisory committee and has failed to outline a programme of agricultural policy in Canada.
That is something which is much needed in Canada at this time.
Statistics were given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to surplus wheat in Canada and other exporting countries at this time. Therefore I have taken time to consider the prices of wheat in some of these other countries. To begin with, according to the Searle grain report of March 4, 1942, the price in the United Kingdom, which imports a great deal of wheat, is placed at $1,901 for the home producer. The report states:
The price of homegrown wheat in the United Kingdom will be increased by about 18 cents a bushel for the 1942 crop. The new price will be equal to about $1.90f per bushel in Canadian funds.
The price of wheat in the United States, which also has a very considerable surplus, is set out by Mr. R. M. Evans, administrator of agricultural adjustment and conservation in the United States Department of Agriculture. I was privileged to listen to a speech by Mr. Evans in the Chateau Laurier last winter. He has stated that commodity loans are made to producers who have complied with their acreage allotments. These loans are based upon So per cent of the parity price for the commodity. For wheat this has meant a loan rate of $1.15 a bushel for No. 2 wheat at Chicago. On March 7, May wheat was quoted at Chicago at $1,291. It was quoted at Winnipeg at 79J cents or a difference of 50J cents a bushel.
We have had the united requests of the western pools, western governments, municipal unions, western boards of trade and other' organizations representing every walk of life west of the great lakes asking for an initial payment of at least $1 a bushel. Some of them used the parity of 1913-14 which was $1.20 a bushel, and T have already quoted the parity of 1926-29, which was $1.42 a bushel. Reference
has been made to the proposal of the line elevators. They suggested:
(a)	An initial payment for farmers delivering their 1942 wheat crop to the Canadian wheat board of $1.22J per bushel basis one northern delivered Fort William or Vancouver.
(b)	That the government accept delivery of 350,000,000 bushels of the 1942 wheat crop on this price basis.
(c)	That deliveries and sales of the 1942 wheat crop be segregated from the carryover of past years and the carryover be reserved to meet post-war and unforeseen war requirements.
That is in keeping with the previous suggestion of that great British leader, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, and the man who was a great figure in the last war, Mr. Lloyd George, that there should be established a surplus to be held until after the war, which surplus would prove a great talking point when many of the nations of Europe would be so hungry.
I listened this afternoon to the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) attempt to take credit to himself and the other Liberal members for all that was worth while in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He said that members had gone home and made little of it, telling the people that they would never be paid under that scheme. I have no idea to whom he referred, but I know I have never heard of any member discussing that undertaking in that Way. Some time before I became a member of this house I advocated some form of crop insurance, and I think that is a step in the right direction. I will be quite frank and say that in many places, including this house, I have criticized the administration of the act. I think I was right in doing so because I believe it could be greatly improved upon, especially the administration during the first year of its operation. But it was a step in the right direction and, as the pool delegation pointed out while asking for a higher price for wheat, the scheme should be broadened so that it would be of more use to the people in the west.
The hon. member went on to refer to the 70 cents a bushel paid for wheat, and the 30 cents a bushel which was paid on an acreage basis. However, the farmer in my neighbourhood does not get 70 cents a bushel; he gets only 51 or 52 cents. Moreover, I submit that the acreage reduction bonus or the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has no relationship with the price of wheat produced. Perhaps it could not be called charity, but it is a means of providing for those who do not produce the commodity and, therefore, has no proper connection with the higher price we are asking for so urgently, a price higher than that contained in the statement given to us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the house on the bill at this particular time, other than to state that I shall support this amendment to 'provide a parity price for agricultural products, and especially for wheat.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak again until these bills had gone to committee but in view of the fact that the resolution now before the house in the form of an amendment is stated in terms which do not place before the house in a proper manner what actually did take place when the farmers' delegation from western Canada was here, I desire to address a few words to the house before the vote is taken. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time, but be it resolved that the disregarding by this parliament of the modest representations made by western agriculture for a parity price for all agricultural products and an initial wheat payment of at least $1 per bushel for No. 1 northern basis Fort William is contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
The first thing to which I should like to call attention is the fact that this does not refer to the government of Canada; it does not refer to the Department of Trade and Commerce, the minister of which department is introducing this bill, and it does not refer to the Department of Agriculture. It is not a condemnation of any one of those three. It says:
. . . this bill be not now read a second time, but be it resolved that the disregarding by this parliament of the modest representations made by western agriculture for a parity price for all agricultural products and an initial wheat payment of at least $1 per bushel for No. 1 northern basis Fort William is contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
I scarcely know, as a member of the government or as a minister of the department responsible for two of the bills before the house, whether I should speak on behalf of the whole parliament in asking that this parliament should not condemn itself, or whether I should speak only on behalf of the legislation itself. Probably it would be best if I were to place before the house exactly the representations that were made by the farmers of western Canada when they were here and also, as nearly as I can, the position taken by those members of the government who met the delegation. I shall try to leave with the house some idea of the understanding with which the farm delegation left Ottawa.

In order to do that, I think I should refer to the last occasion upon which I as a representative of the government, spoke to the delegation in Ottawa. The proceedings before the delegation when government members were present were taken down by Hansard reporters, and there is an exact report of what occurred. When I was addressing the delegates just before they closed their last business meeting with the government, I made the following statement as reported on page 61:
I am pleased that at your first meeting yesterday you had the opportunity of meeting nearly all the members of the government and that in the afternoon you met all the members of the wheat committee of council, and, this afternoon, three of those members. For I consider it my responsibility to go before the wheat committee of council and also to go before the full council and submit your views presented on this occasion as I have understood them. And I may say I intend to do that. But let me repeat what I said yesterday. Do not go away from the meeting understanding because I have promised to submit your views you are going to get all that you have asked for. Your representations will be made to the whole government and will be considered by the whole government. Legislation will be necessary to effect whatever we decide to do. Any legislative bill introduced into council as a result of discussions in the w'heat committee relating to the price of wheat must of necessity be introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but it will be considered and passed on by the members of the government, and it will be the decision of the whole government which will finally rule in the matter.
I think the delegates when they left understood perfectly what the relationship was from that time on between the government and the delegation itself with reference particularly to the matter of the wheat price which was to be established in connection with this legislation. I could go on to read succeeding pages, but I shall not take the time to do so to-night. In these succeeding pages I have asked them definitely what it is they desire to have, and in these pages they have set this out. One thing they are very definite about is that they would like to have a SI advance on wheat. Another thing they are very definite about is that they would like to have an increased payment on one or two occasions during the year, to bring the entire amount received for their wheat, during that twelve months of 1942, up to what they term parity price. When I asked them definitely if they meant by parity price $1.41 a bushel, which was the average price for 1926-29, the president of the wheat pool explained to me and the delegation that they were prepared to accept what the statistics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce would determine to be parity price. In other words, they went away believing that what they had asked for was a $1 advance on wheat, plus

Wheat Board Act
payments during the year which would bring the total payments made, following the 1942 crop and within that twelve-months' period, up to what would be agreed upon as parity price.

The petition which was brought by the delegation outlines their requests perhaps better than anything else, and I should therefore like to deal with the different sections of that petition, seven in number. The petition was signed by upwards of 185,000 people of Saskatchewan. The delegation of four hundred was a delegation from Saskatchewan alone, but they had asked representatives of the farm organizations in Alberta and representatives of the farm organizations in Manitoba to accompany them. The petition was signed in the province of Saskatchewan by some 185,000 people. They were not all farmers. About one-third of the delegation which came to Ottawa came from the urban districts, and from Moose Jaw, Regina and Saskatoon the mayors of these cities came to Ottawa with the delegation. Therefore, while the delegation was not all farmers, I would agree with the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas) when he said this afternoon that this was a representative delegation from Saskatchewan, representative not only of the farmers but of most of the people of that province.
The first thing they asked was that the government recognize and accept the principle of parity price for all agricultural products. The first statement in the amendment that has been proposed is:
. . . this bill be not now read a second time, but be it resolved that the disregarding by this parliament of the modest representations made by western agriculture for a parity price for all agricultural products and an initial wheat payment of at least $1 per bushel for No. 1 northern basis Fort William is contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
I do not expect that this house is going to disregard that request which was made by the farmers of western Canada. But whether this house disregards it or not, the government of Canada has not disregarded it nor has the Department of Agriculture nor the Depart-44561-77
ment of Trade and Commerce. Every possible consideration under the circumstances was given to that representation, and may I say that what has been done up to date with regard to most of the products with which the western farmers are concerned is not so far away from what was asked as some members would like to lead the house to believe.
For example, parity for butter, which is one of the very important products of Saskatchewan is 36-5 cents a pound. This differs from my yesterday's figure because I used the average price for 1926-29 yesterday, while this is the figure adjusted for changes in purchasing power. The price of butter is 35-5 cents a pound. Therefore at the present time there is really only one cent of difference between what was declared to be parity and the price which butter is actually bringing at Montreal at present-and prices in Saskatchewan range back from the price at Montreal.
Cheese is a-product with which they are not so much concerned in Saskatchewan, but the delegation made it very plain when they were here that they were concerned not only with themselves but with all the farmers of Canada, and that they wanted parity for all the farmers of Canada. Parity for cheese is 18 cents a pound. These and all succeeding parity prices are calculated on the same basis as butter. The ceiling price actually set for cheese-and cheese has been maintained within a cent or two of it-is 25 cents a pound. That is seven cents above parity. Is anyone in this house going to conclude that the government have paid no attention to the representations of the western delegation that we should have parity for agricultural prices when here are two of the most important dairy products which are marketed in the Dominion of Canada, one selling within one cent of parity and the other up to seven cents over parity? I am sure that the house will agree that the government did pay some attention to the representations of the delegation, and that we paid some attention to the representations which the house has made to the government from time to time.
Coming to the next one on the list, hogs, the parity price in Toronto is 11-09 cents; in Winnipeg, 10 cents. On the market in Toronto the day before yesterday hogs were selling at 11-63 cents- and parity is 11-09 cents. In Winnipeg hogs have been selling consistently above 10 cents ever since the agreement entered into last fall. Again, are we going to say that either the Department of Agriculture or the government of Canada or this house has paid no attention to the representations made to the effect that we should have parity in hog prices?

But that particular item illustrates, Mr. Speaker, a fact in relation to this whole question which never yet has been placed squarely before this house. Hon. members have said from time to time that the reason why prices of wheat are not higher is that there is not a demand for our wheat. A year ago the reason why the price of flax was not higher was that there was not a demand for flax. The ceiling price was set at $1.64, and no farmer in western Canada would grow flax at present for $1.64. There would not be a production of it excepting on those lands which had been prepared for flax and which farmers were going to put into that crop whether they expected to make any return from it or not. But things have happened since last year. We have a demand for vegetable oil. We have a shortage of vegetable oils which cannot be met from any importations. We must produce whatever vegetable oils we require in addition to those which we have already imported. So that there is a demand for flax, and immediately it arose the government of Canada said, "We are prepared to pay $2.25 a bushel in order to get it grown in Canada"-20 cents more than the average price for 1926-29, and 29 cents higher, I believe, than the parity price as stated in the figures which have been prepared' for me in the department.
That brings me to those grain products for which I cannot claim there is at present a parity price in this country; they are oats, barley and rye.
In so far as rye is concerned, it is not a grain which is produced in great quantities in any part of Canada. It is grown in the west by a limited number of farmers and over a limited area, more particularly on the lighter soils. It does not concern the income of any considerable number of farmers in western Canada.
Barley and oats are much more important crops. The suggested parity price for barley is 69-7 cents, and the ceiling is 64J cents; that is, the ceiling is almost five cents below the parity price. But, Mr. Speaker, there is another point in relation to that which I wish to make after giving the figures for oats. For oats, 57-3 cents is parity and 51| cents is the ceiling. There is a difference of under six cents a bushel. Those two grains are produced largely for feeding purposes in Canada,

and are directly related to the live stock products with which I have been dealing. I believe I would be safe in saying that at least ninety per cent of the grain which is grown in Canada in those two classifications is fed to live stock in Canada, and nearly all of it is fed on the farms where it is grown. So this price is not one which represents a return to the farmer for the great volume of the coarse grains. The prices which represent the returns are the prices of those live stock products which I have already given to the house, most of which are away above parity. I again submit that the statement made in the amendment is not one with which hon. members in any quarter of this house can agree if they are going to take the facts into consideration.
That brings me to wheat. Everyone in this house, everyone in the country admits that wheat is not at a parity price, and I believe, in spite of what has been said by some hon. members, that every member of the delegation-I would be very much surprised if any of them said otherwise-went home believing that they were not going to get all that *they asked for wheat. There is every reason why they should have believed that, and there is every reason at the same time why they should have impressed upon the government the importance of bringing the wheat price to parity at as early a date as possible. But let me repeat, I do not believe that any one of them went home expecting that they were going to get all that they asked for in relation to wheat. What else could the remark which I made to them have meant, when I reviewed to them all of these seven requests which they made, indicated to them those which we had already dealt with to a considerable extent, indicated also some which we would not be able to deal with as they had asked us to deal with them, and then said that the most important thing for which they had asked in their submission was a price for wheat; and we spent most of our time discussing that particular policy. They went away with the idea definitely in their minds, I believe, that everything that could be done for them under the circumstances would be done, though not all that they asked for would be done.

speechtext:
There were 467. I have a group of returns here covering the greater part of Saskatchewan, and another group covering Manitoba and another for Alberta. They demonstrate that under the arrangements which have been made for prairie farm assistance, as passed by this house three years ago -and in municipalities such as this by far the greater part of the income is derived under prairie farm assistance-the result has been a levelling of the amount received up to about what is required in a municipality in order to make it possible for people to remain off relief; and that was the objective in framing of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It has proven itself in the second poorest crop year we have experienced in recent years.
When the farm delegation came here they first congratulated us upon the fact that we had put the Prairie Farm Assistance Act upon the statute books, and then asked us to increase that assistance. I placed these figures before them, and after I had done so they did not repeat their request. They did say, "We want prairie farm assistance continued," and they also said they would like to have it converted into insurance. I told them there was only one reason why we did not convert it into insurance; that was the fact that we were informed that it was ultra vires of this parliament to pass legislation with regard to insurance of this kind. I believe that whole question was threshed out at the time hail insurance was established in the western provinces. We asked the federal government to establish it. The matter was looked into, it was determined that the federal government could not do it, so the western provinces established hail insurance.
When this legislation was before the house three years ago I appeared before a committee in the other place, and on that occasion the then Conservative leader there, Mr. Meighen, asked me the direct question: "Is this insurance?" I said I did not think so.
He asked, "Is it intra vires?" I replied, "I am not a constitutional lawyer, but the legal advisers in my department say that it is intra vires." He said he had some doubts about it but that they had a legal adviser in the other place, at that time Mr. O'Connor; and he turned to Mr. O'Connor and asked what he thought about it. Mr. O'Connor said he had some doubts as to whether it was intra vires, but he added, 'It is the kind of legislation that ought to be passed by some body for western Canada. I think it should be passed, and if it is ultra vires that can be proved in the courts." So the bill went through the committee with only one dissenting voice; it was passed in the other place, and became law. I told the story to the farmers who were here and said I did not think we could introduce legislation in the form of insurance, but we did intend to maintain this legislation upon the statute books for this year at least, and that as long as I was Minister of Agriculture I hoped that it would be retained on the statute books. They applauded that remark, and as far as this point was concerned they carried that idea home with them.
I give that recital in order to indicate to this house that the farmers who came here from western Canada were not misled. They were given a complete understanding of the situation, and they returned home knowing pretty well what we intended to do in connection with the various recommendations which were placed before us. Let me read those recommendations. I have dealt in full with some of them already, but I should like to place them all on Hansard. The first is:
1.	That the government recognize and accept the principle of parity prices for all agricultural products.
I have already indicated that the government had the average prices of 1926-29 as an objective. The next request was:
2.	That no price ceiling should be established on agricultural commodities below parity levels which may be established by the dominion bureau of statistics.
I have dealt with that, indicating the extent to which we have departed from it. In essence the only departure has been in connection with wheat. As to the other products, they are practically at parity, or over parity or in a position where the returns to the farmer do not come from the direct sale of the product. Then:
3.	That equitable delivery quotas on wheat should be established and continued as long as required.
In this regard I told the farmers that this was the policy of the government; that it was established two years ago; that it was still
Wheat Board Act

maintained, and that, as far as I knew, it would be maintained as long as conditions warranted. Then:
4.	That the initial payment on all wheat delivered to the wheat board should be not less than $1 per bushel, basis 1 northern in store Fort William, and that the final settlement should be made on the basis of parity prices above referred to.
I think I have discussed that point fully, but should add that it was agreed this was asked for the 1942 crop. The next request was:
5.	That the carryover of wheat as at 31st July, 1941, should be regarded as a national emergency war reserve, and that all sales made by the wheat board after 31st July, 1941, should be credited to the current season's deliveries.
That was a request which had its origin in this house. Whatever hon. gentlemen opposite may say as to who originated the idea, I think it can be truly said that it came some two or three years ago from the Liberal members on this side, and since that time it has been taken up and advocated by the pools. I explained fully to the delegation that when this request was made for the first time by the pool organizations, in August of last year, I had brought their representations back to Ottawa, but that by the time they were presented here it was found that a very considerable part of the wheat which had been marketed prior to that time had been sold outright, and that therefore anything in the way of payment on participation certificates in relation to that wheat would not benefit a very considerable number of the farmers of the west. So it was suggested by the government that instead of making a payment on that basis, in order to give greater income to the farmers of western Canada the payment should be made on the basis of an acreage income payment. That acreage income payment was estimated at 120,000,000, or exactly 10 cents a bushel on 200,000,000 bushels of wheat, which at that time we considered would probably be delivered in western Canada.
In other words, it was agreed by the government that the income from wheat was too low, partly because of the fact that we had asked farmers to reduce their wheat acreage, and partly because of the fact that there was a poor crop last year, and that that income should be increased. While we were not prepared under the circumstances to increase it by declaring all of the carryover to be a reserve, and then paying their participation on the sale price of the wheat in 1941, still we were prepared to deliver upwards of $20,000,000 to the farmers on the basis of 75 cents an acre on half their cultivated acreage. That is being done. It was explained to the farmers, and that explanation will be found in this volume
(Mr. Gardiner.]
I have before me on my desk at the present time.
Then No. 6:
6.	That suitable amendments should be introduced to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so that an adequate and practical crop insurance scheme may be established irrespective of market prices prevailing or the number of townships suffering crop failure.
There is only one part of that recommendation which I have not explained to the house, as I explained it to the delegates at that time, and that is the last phrase of it. This has reference to the number of townships suffering from crop failure, and the suggestion that that number should be cut out of the legislation altogether. At the present time the legislation says that you must have 171 townships in Saskatchewan with less than five bushels to the acre before you can declare a crop failure area in that province. I believe the figure for Alberta is 90 or 91, and for Manitoba it is 50. The proposal here is that we cut those figures out and make it so that an area could be declared to be a crop failure area, even though it consisted of only one township.
I explained to the delegation that there is only one reason, in addition to the one I have already explained (insurance), why we based this act on the township, and that is that we wished to prevent areas, or single farms consisting of poor soil, or having farmers upon them who could not make good land grow crops, from drawing under this legislation every year. In other words, if a township averages over twelve bushels to the acre, we estimate that- the farmers in that area ought to be able to grow enough wheat or enough of other crops to get along. It will be remembered that wheat is only a barometer under this act. The payments are not made on wheat; they are made on cultivated acreage, even if there is no wheat grown on the farm at all. Wheat, may I repeat, is used only as a barometer.
So what we say to them is that if it is possible to grow an average of more than twelve bushels to the acre in a township, then the weather has been such in that township that the government should not be called upon to pay any assistance there. This means that if there were half a dozen farmers in there who, irrespective of weather conditions, are not able to grow twelve bushels to the acre, then there must be something wrong either with the land they are farming or with their methods of farming. In either case it is not something over which the farmer himself has no control.
Then, when it comes to a matter of dealing with large areas we say that if four or five

Wheat Board Act
townships were made an area which could be declared a crop failure area, it is possible in any of the provinces of western Canada to find an area of four or five townships of submarginal lands which would come under this legislation every year. So we have said that there must be a comparatively large area declared in, and that there must be within the townships themselves a low average before they will be permitted in. All of these things were explained to the delegation which was here.
After the explanation was made, a representative of the municipal association from south of the city of Regina came to the platform and stated he wished to place before the government three resolutions passed by the municipal association of Saskatchewan. One representation was to the effect that we should not allow anyone to be paid who had grown over twelve bushels to the acre on an average. I said to him that there were thousands of farmers in western Canada who grow wheat only on the best land they have, only on the best prepared summer-fallow they have, and that those men will probably always have more than twelve bushels to the acre, on a very limited acreage. The same men may have no coarse grains at all, because their coarse grains are grown on spring ploughing, and it requires a great deal more rainfall to grow a crop of any kind, as every farmer knows, on spring ploughing than it does on summer-fallow. So he might be entirely without coarse grains. His pasture may be poor because there has been no rain.
I repeat-and I stated this to the farm delegation-that wheat is only the barometer in connection with this act. Those who have said, from the other side of the house, that it is not altogether correct to say that payments made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are payments made on wheat, are quite right in their statement. You can draw under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, even if you do not grow an acre of wheat. As was said by someone yesterday-I do not remember who it was-one of the functions of the act is to encourage the farmer to go out of wheat and into coarse grains. That was one of the reasons why we did not tie the payments to the wheat crop, but rather tried to tie them to the total acreage a farmer might be farming.
The next request-and this is the last one -is in these words:

(a)	to conserve the fertility of our soil;

and since these objectives may involve an increasing degree of control and regulation, including international agreement, such changes should be made in our agricultural policy as may be necessary to achieve these objectives.
I said, with regard to this, that we had already been doing something with respect to the conservation of the fertility of our soil. We have done that through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, through the encouragement to summer-fallow, through the encouragement to grow roughage in connection with some of the summer-fallow1-and this practice was criticized yesterday from the opposite side of the house-rather than having summer-fallow which would require keeping all of the soil black at all times. All these things are being encouraged to-day. And they agreed-at least no one raised any objection to my explanation-with what was being done under that legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to repeat what has been stated so far in this debate and my remarks will be extremely brief. I just want to bring to the notice of the house some of the background of wheat production so that the lessons which have been learned through hard experience will not go into the discard but be of use in the future.
Long ago, in 1813, the hardy highland Scotsmen of the Selkirk clan came into this country by way of Hudson bay and settled in the Red river valley. In order to sustain life they started cultivating the land, and there started a struggle which has gone on to this present day. They came and had many difficulties to face. The winters were long and severe. The seed which they brought with them was unsuitable. The traders, the Indians and the wild animals were their enemies. They suffered from drought, grasshoppers and frost. Hardships indeed were their lot.
But toward the end of the last centuiy conditions considerably improved. They secured hardier varieties of seed. There were improved milling processes, and great railways stretched across this continent running from coast to coast. A new era seemed to have opened. People came into the west from eastern Canada, from Great Britain, from every country of the world, and westward the tide of civilization moved, through the forests,
TMr. Gardiner.]
across the swollen streams and over the great prairie region until there was land cultivated right within sight of the Rocky mountains.
In 1886 some 11 million bushels of wheat were produced. In 11)00 that had grown to [DOT]14 million bushels, and we have heard that a year ago we produced 540 million bushels. All down from those days to the present day the farmers have had to struggle for a living, so that they have not had reserves. They have no landed estate to fall back upon but must live from year to year almost upon the earnings of each year.
Their struggles were first with the railways. The farmers drove long distances to sell their loads of grain and often had to take them back home again. They had difficulty in getting permission to sell across the platform. They had difficulties in getting storage. Then, when the elevator companies came they had trouble with them over grades, weights, overages, prices, the mixing of grain and things of that kind. The Manitoba Grain Act of 1900 solved many of their difficulties, but they were soon up against new problems. Those who were handling the grain united to protect their own profits, and so those who were growing the grain were also forced to unite in order to bring their bargaining power to bear at one point in order to survive. They did unite under such men as Peter Dayman, John Miller, John Sibbald, E. A. Partridge, and W. R. Motherwell. These men were leaders in that movement. They united the farmers into organizations and even went so far as to set up their own grain company, with their own elevators and mills, in the hope of cutting out the profit of the middleman and having the members of their organization survive. This brought them into sharp clash with the grain exchange, which had then been organized, and from that day to this the grain exchange has been very unpopular among the producers.
Then we have what was called the siege of Ottawa. In December, 1910, some eight hundred people came to this national capital. They marched, four abreast, to the parliament buildings on a cold winter morning; they entered the then House of Commons; they crowded the galleries; they filled the floor of the house. The Speaker introduced some twenty of them, and they told their grievances, the grievances of that day, to the members who were crowded in the chamber wherever they could find seats. They made out a good case and they convinced the people of the east of their difficulties.
Another striking event was the bringing to the west, I believe by various newspaper companies, of a man named Aaron Sapiro. Wherever he went he attracted great audiences, because he talked to them of the simple things which they could understand.

Wheat Board Act
He tolld them of the results of the cooperative movement, how when he first went around on organization work, the children of the producers were in rags and appeared to be undernourished; but the cooperatives were started, and the next time he went around, their conditions had improved. The lesson of such experiences surely is that there must be an organization to protect the interests of the growers, that that organization must be strong, and that cooperation will give the maximum results; it will provide the producer with more nearly the value of his product than will any other form of organized effort. Surely in the future we must be guided by the experiences which were so hardly gained by those pioneers in the movement.
Until recent times it has been very easy to sell wheat. I well remember hearing a minister of trade and commerce say that our high protein content wheat would easily sell itself. But such is no longer the situation. Of the countries to which we sold wheat, some are now our enemies, others are overrun by our enemies, and our only remaining market is Great Britain, of whose purchases we have only a limited share. Therefore this government was placed fairly against the problem, would they protect and preserve the farming industry, or would they let it go into bankruptcy? If the farming industry failed, food products would not be supplied which might be badly needed in times of famine. If the farming industry failed, one and a half million people would be thrown on the relief rolls of this country.
The industry has a strong administrative organization; it is equiped with great terminal facilities at the head of the lakes; it has worked out a great transportation system. These things must be preserved; and this government decided to preserve the farming industry by support from the treasury. They supported the price of grain. As the minister has just explained, they put into operation the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. This is to some extent an insurance act. During the two years of its operation they have collected by their one per cent tax on all grain four million dollars from the farmers of Canada, and they have paid out eleven and a half million dollars. This assistance has helped a great many people, but the act is sadly in need of amending. Every day I get letters from people who are heart-broken because their bonuses fail to come through. Of course the farmers of the west are not chartered accountants, and in some cases the trouble may be due to discrepancies. But there are still farmers who have not received a bonus of any kind for the past year, and they are badly in need of it. Thus, the secretary of the United Farmers of Alberta at Retlaw writes:
We are about at wit's end to know what to do as every official surely knows about it by now.
Many people are in real desperate circumstances and it is soon time to be on the land again. . . .
Farmers still wait at post offices hoping for a payment to come and only to turn away bitter and discouraged, wishing the reduction scheme had have never been thought of.
Harry Malm,
Secretary.
I find that 90-cent price for wheat will automatically cancel the bonus which was formerly paid in cases of crop failure where the yield is from eight to twelve bushels per acre. This, it seems to me, will be a great blow to the people of the west. I want to take this opportunity to urge the minister so to amend the act that this shall not happen, because those small yields will not sustain a decent standard of living on the farm, and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act will not perform its function, will not give the help it should give, if that bracket is cancelled out.
The farmers of the west appreciate, I am sure, even the twenty-cent advance in the price of wheat. They appreciate these bonuses, although they are the cause of much heartache and disappointment because of their slowness in coming through. They appreciate the fact that speculation in grain will come to an end and that if the price of grain should go up, the farmers will be benefited. I am convinced that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) have done their very best for the benefit of the farmers of the west, and that no ministers could have done more. But I do say that even these additions will be only an instalment of what should come. They will not relieve the distress which the wheat producer is having, and they will not equalize sacrifice in this country.
Recently the war loan was floated. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) should be congratulated upon the splendid response to that loan. But what does it show? One city in the east contributed as much as two whole provinces in the west. That shows where the money lies, and it demonstrates that the pleas which we are making for improved conditions are justified.
We must remember that Canada is one of the democratic nations, one of the great nations, made great by the wheat producer and his contribution in making this country the bread-basket of the world. We are one of the united nations that are fighting against the barbarous nazis and the treacherous and ruthless Japanese, and we realize that Canada's contribution has been magnificent. We must make a balanced contribution through a programme which will defend our own shores and help in distant fields of battle, so that victoiy may come in the least possible time.

Questions
We must so act that those who are watching us in the present day, and those future generations which will look back upon what we have done, will be astonished at the greatness of our contribution. We must struggle and sacrifice and expand that contribution, and falter not-
Lest a thousand ages find us Frustrate at our highest chance,
Lest the hour of trial reveal us False to our inheritance.
